Latest Update: How to Address Common Causes of Knee Pain While Cycling

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a cyclist, you probably know that you should always listen to your knees and the messages they send when they’re not so happy.
  • Recent findings suggest that fortunately, the culprit is often an easy fix, but the first step is to identify what may be causing your knee pain.
  • In a recent development, any spontaneous twinges of crank-stopping knee pain may feel like they come out of no where, when actually they’re just the first noticeable symptoms of a long-brewing problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a cyclist, you probably know that you should always listen to your knees and the messages they send when they’re not so happy. These messages show up as aches and pains, and they’re common among those who ride. While research suggests cycling can actually help you avoid knee pain later in life, other studies indicate it still affects about 15 to 30 percent of cyclists.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, the culprit is often an easy fix, but the first step is to identify what may be causing your knee pain. For example, you may be overtraining and pushing your body harder than it’s used to, straining your connective tissues and causing inflammation and pain.

In a recent development, any spontaneous twinges of crank-stopping knee pain may feel like they come out of no where, when actually they’re just the first noticeable symptoms of a long-brewing problem. This generally stems from equipment and/or bike position complications, indicates bike-fit specialist Michael Veal of BikeDynamics in Warwickshire, England.

According to recent reports, “Many cyclists are forever tinkering with their position, looking for that elusive perfect position,” he says. But what feels just right for a few pedal strokes around the block can end up feeling pretty wrong after 70 miles of roads. A good bike fit is essential for preventing most causes of knee pain.

For more guidance on what your knee pain means and strategies to avoid it, read on.

WANT MORE INFO ON BIKE FIT? CHECK OUT OUR EXCLUSIVE PROGRAM!

To help you figure out where to start, here are the most common types of cycling knee pain and the ways in which your bike fit may contribute to each symptom.

According to recent reports, if your knee hurts right on the cap (or patella), it’s typically because of your quads. The four quadricep muscles attach to the shin via the patella, and when you’re putting force into your pedal stroke, these muscles deliver that force across the knee joint.

Sources indicate that your bike set-up can help with this problem. Determine whether adjusting your saddle height, saddle fore and aft, and/or crank length could alleviate the glitch. Working with a professional bike fitter can be extremely helpful in addressing this type of knee pain.

Sources indicate that “A saddle that is too low will keep your knee angle too tight at the top of the stroke, which increases the shear forces pulling the patella against the femur, which in turn increases the likelihood of tendonitis and harmful stresses in the cartilage behind the kneecap,” Veal indicates. “Likewise when the cranks are too long for your leg length, the knee joint is also too tight at the top of the stroke.”.

According to recent reports, how low is too low for a saddle? “For a quick reference to check if your saddle is the right height, have a seat and rest your heel on the pedal with the pedal in the 6 o’clock position,” indicates fit specialist and physical therapist Sara Bresnick, founder of Pedal Power Training Solutions in Medford, Massachusetts. “The knee of that leg should be straight. That equates to a 20- to 25-degree knee bend when clipped in.”.

Riding with your saddle too far forward also can cause knee pain in the front, indicates Veal. “Your saddle should be positioned so the tibial tuberosity—or the bony bit below the kneecap—is directly above the ball of the foot, which in turn should be above the pedal spindle,” she says.

Also, be mindful of your form. Significant-gear mashing, climbing in monster gears, and hard sprinting (especially if you’re not conditioned for it) can put undue stress on the knee and cause this type of pain.

If you do achieve a solid bike fit and avoid these common mistakes, and pain still persists, focus on stretching the quads to find relief.

Recent findings suggest that pain behind the knee is less common than pain in the front, and is generally easier to trace back to a culprit: over-extending the knee, claims Bresnick. Your saddle is too high or too far back. “Try lowering the saddle a bit or moving it forward a bit in relation to the handlebars,” she says.

This pain is also more common among cyclists who spend a lot of time on fixed-gear bikes; When you ride fixed, you use your hamstrings to decelerate your pedal stroke, which can put the biceps femoris tendon (a hamstring muscle that runs down the back of your leg toward the outside of your knee) under too much load and irritate it. Giving your legs a break with some freewheeling now and then can also help.

If pain sticks around after making bike adjustments, try stretching the hamstrings regularly and avoid frequent out-of-saddle riding.

Recent findings suggest that when you feel pain on the inner (or medial sides) of your knees, look down at your feet: Cleat placement is often a culprit, says Veal. Your cleat position affects your Q-factor, which dictates how far apart your feet are laterally when pedaling.

Ideally, the spacing should be that the loads from your knees to your pedals are traveling vertically without pushing the knee inward or outward, which stresses the ligaments on either side of your knee and can lead to pain.

Cleats positioned too close to the insides of your cycling shoes increase the distance between your feet, which can stress the inside collateral ligaments and cause pain in the inner (or medial) sides of your knees.

Too much float in your pedals also can cause medial knee pain. A little float—about 4.5 degrees—is all you need to be comfortable and keep your knees from getting stressed.

According to recent reports, while a professional can help you adjust cleat positioning, you can also have someone take a slow-motion video you riding on a trainer, recording movement from the front of the bike. Look for asymmetry between your left and right side.

It has been revealed that if you still feel pain on the inside of your knee after aligning your cleats, especially if it is a burning pain at rest or sharp pain when you start to walk or step up or down, you may have a type of bursitis. This pain typically improves with a warmup and stretching of the hip flexors and adductors (inner thighs).

Pain on the outer (or lateral) sides of the knees is often caused by iliotibial (IT) band syndrome—a stabbing pain that happens when the IT band (a fibrous connective tissue band that runs from the hip along the thigh to the tibia) becomes stressed and inflamed.

IT band problems can appear to come out of nowhere, and hurt most when the knee is at 20- to 30-degrees of flexion, like when you approach the 6 o’clock position and start to come back up.

Recent findings suggest that “Misaligned cleats that cause the foot to be excessively toed in can cause this,” indicates Veal. So can cleats that are placed too far to the outsides of the shoes, causing too narrow of a stance on the bike.

If you think the cleats on your bike are misaligned, take your bike in for an adjustment. (A slow-mo video of you riding from the front can also help you see if your cleat positioning is to blame!).

Industry observers note that of course, what you do on your bike will also go a long way to promoting or alleviating knee pain. Here are some tips to assure it’s the latter.

Recent findings suggest that just as with most sports, a little warmup to get blood flowing and muscles primed is a good idea—so don’t skip it! As a general rule, aim for at least 15 minutes of moderate spinning before you attack the local climb or go hard on the flats.

Look at video of the pros in action, and you’ll notice their rapid and fluid pedal strokes. Try this drill to improve your pedal stroke: The next time you are going up your favorite climb, use a gear at least two teeth lower (thus easier) than usual. This higher cadence is easier on your joints. Think about making round circles as you pedal, not ovals.

Industry observers note that your first ride back after any extended amount of time off shouldn’t be five hours long. Instead, start with a lower mileage and build slowly.

Sources indicate that your body likes consistency, so when you alter equipment, your knees often protest. Whether you get a newly introduced bike, new shoes, new pedals, or change stem length, go easy at first to give yourself time to adapt.

According to recent reports, riding in 40-degree weather with red, chapped knees is a recipe for trouble. Pros routinely cover their legs in training when the temperature is below 60 degrees—that’s why knee warmers exist!

According to recent reports, while each individual’s tolerance will differ, there’s certainly no harm in keeping muscles and joints warm. By using warmers, you can easily slip them off mid-ride if you start to warm up.

Take note of what gear works best in certain weather conditions, so you can repeat on future rides.

According to recent reports, if knee pain persists, consider getting a professional bike fit. And no, we’re not talking about when a salesperson sets your seat height at purchase.

A professional bike fit should be an in-depth experience with a professionally trained fitter that includes an interview process, off-bike flexibility testing, and on-bike measurements and adjustments. Yes, it’s an investment (usually at least $200), but it’s worth it to ride pain-free. It could end up being the best money you ever spent on your cycling habit.

Industry observers note that if you’re still experiencing cycling knee pain after doing everything mentioned above, including a professional bike fit, it may be caused by muscle imbalances instead—like weak glutes, hips, or core. It’s best to consult with a sports medicine physician and/or physical therapist to find the right course of treatment for you.

John Vasudevan, M.D. is an associate professor at the University of Pennsylvania. He is board-certified in Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation and Sports Medicine. He is a Team Physician for UPenn Athletics and  medical director of the Broad Street Run and Philadelphia Distance Run, and previously for the Rock 'n' Roll Half-Marathon and Tri-Rock Triathlon in Philadelphia. He is a director of the running and endurance Sports Medicine Program at Penn Medicine. Dr. Vasudevan provides non-operative management of musculoskeletal conditions affecting athletes and active individuals of all levels, and combines injury rehabilitation with injury prevention. He utilizes a variety of ultrasound-guided procedures and regenerative approaches such as platelet-rich plasma and percutaneous ultrasonic tenotomy. He sees patients at the Penn Medicine and the Philadelphia Veterans Administration hospital. Dr. Vasudevan attended medical school at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison. After his Transitional Year in Tucson, Arizona, he went to residency in PM&R at Thomas Jefferson University in Philadelphia and onwards to Stanford University for his fellowship in Sports Medicine. He has been in practice at the University of Pennsylvania since 2012.

#137035. Tech Report: Trek’s Latest Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

Tech Report: Trek’s Latest Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that this Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here.
  • Sources indicate that if you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the fresh Domane belongs on your list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that this Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here. Next, I want to hear what you think. Bicycling members can continue the discussion with me on Discord, where I’ll answer questions and hear how the Domane works for riders beyond my test. The invitation appears after the review.

Sources indicate that if you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the fresh Domane belongs on your list. It feels more eager under power than previous versions, while keeping the stability and confidence that have always made the bike good at everyday riding.

Sources indicate that the version I’d point most people toward is the $4,200 SL 6 AXS. It gets the same geometry, tire clearance, and basic frame features as the expensive SLR models, along with electronic shifting and carbon wheels. The SLR saves weight and opens the door to Trek’s Project One customization. Those are real advantages, but they don’t make it a fundamentally different bike.

I tested the $11,499 SLR 9 AXS 2x. It weighed 16.3 pounds in size M. The bike I’d recommend first costs less than half as much.

Sources indicate that BIKE TESTED: Trek Gen. 5 Domane SLR 9 AXS 2xACTUAL WEIGHT 16.3 pounds (Size M, as tested) USE Road, light gravel PRICE AS TESTED $11,499 MODEL PRICE RANGE $2,400 to $11,499; $14,999 limited edition ICON No. 76FRAME ONLY OPTION: Yes. $3,700 (SLR) $2,000 (SL)CUSTOMIZABLE BUILDS Yes, SLR models through Project One SIZES OFFERED XS, S, M, ML, L, XL WEIGHT LIMIT 125 kg/275 lb (bicycle, rider, and cargo) TIRE CLEARANCE 40mm BB STANDARD T47 threaded BRAKE HOSE ROUTING Internal, RCS headset; under bar/stem on most buildsDRIVETRAIN COMPATIBILITY 1x and 2x, electronic shifting only DERAILLEUR HANGER UDH WARRANTY Lifetime, frame and rigid fork, original owner CRASH REPLACEMENT Yes, Trek Carbon Care discounted replacement.

Industry observers note that I’ve ridden every generation of the Domane, including several of the more aggressive RSL versions. Over the years, Trek added adjustable IsoSpeed, front IsoSpeed, internal storage, aero shaping, and hidden cables. The fifth-generation bike pulls back on much of that.

The Gen 5 feels more solid and reactive underfoot than its predecessors. It’s stiffer when I get on the pedals, accelerates with more snap, and climbs with a crispness that used to elude the Domane. In that way, it feels more like a Madone than any previous version.

According to recent reports, it hasn’t lost the stability and confidence that make the Domane a good everyday road bike. I can push it hard down a descent without feeling like I’m taking a test of nerves. The fit is excellent, too. The taller front end should help more riders find a position that’s comfortable and aerodynamic.

Sources indicate that and no, it doesn’t feel slow on 35mm tires. The bike feels quick and responsive. The wider tires are part of what makes it work, not an anchor holding it back.

The original Domane’s signature feature was IsoSpeed, a mechanism that let the seat tube flex to add comfort. Trek developed it over several generations, then removed it from the bike that introduced it.

Sources indicate that the new Domane gets much of its comfort from wider tires at lower pressures, along with frame and seatpost tuning. Most models come with 35mm tires, and the frame clears up to 40mm. Trek says that combination provides enough comfort that IsoSpeed’s remaining benefit isn’t worth its weight and complexity.

Recent findings suggest that isoSpeed still works. Trek told me that with the same 35mm tires, the Gen 4 transmits slightly less vibrational energy than the Gen 5. Trek also indicates the Gen 5 on 35mm tires comes within 5 percent of the Gen 4 on its stock 32mm tires at the rear. At the front, Trek says the two generations perform similarly.

Industry observers note that those are Trek’s test results, not measurements I made. But the decision makes sense to me. Wider tires add traction and capability that IsoSpeed couldn’t provide. Trek decided the system’s remaining comfort advantage wasn’t enough to justify keeping it.

If you own an older Domane, what did IsoSpeed do for you? Did you notice a difference when you moved to wider tires, or do you miss the old system? I’d like to hear what you’ve felt on real roads.

According to Trek’s white paper, the Gen 5 frame is about 292 grams lighter than Gen 4. It also eliminates IsoSpeed and its associated maintenance.

Recent findings suggest that the frame uses a threaded T47 bottom bracket, a round fork steerer, a Universal Derailleur Hanger, and a standard 27.2mm seatpost. For a modern performance bike, there’s not much proprietary weirdness here. That’s a feature.

The internal storage compartment is gone, too. I’ll miss it. It was useful. Trek says its research showed that many Domane owners weren’t using it. The upcoming frame retains fender mounts, top-tube mounts, and frame-bag mounts. I like the trade: less hardware and complexity, with straightforward ways to carry gear when you need to.

Recent findings suggest that the cable routing is another smart compromise. On most models, brake hoses run beneath the two-piece bar and stem before entering the frame at the headset. It looks clean, but changing a bar or stem doesn’t become a major repair job. Fit changes and service matter more to me than hiding every cable at any cost.

According to recent reports, the SL and SLR share the same geometry, tire clearance, seatpost size, bottom bracket, UDH, and general feature set. The SL uses Trek’s 500 Series carbon; the SLR uses lighter 900 Series carbon. Trek says both frames are designed to the same stiffness requirements. The SL supports mechanical drivetrains; the SLR is electronic-shifting only.

Sources indicate that the SLR primarily buys lower weight, access to Trek’s highest-end builds, and the ability to customize components through Project One. Buyers can specify details such as crank length, handlebar width, and stem length. If you’re spending this much on a bike, getting those dimensions right from the factory is a meaningful advantage.

But the SLR doesn’t change the core experience enough to be the obvious choice for most riders. I’d look closely at the $4,200 SL 6 AXS first. It has a carbon frame, electronic shifting, carbon wheels, 40mm tire clearance, and the same accessible fit. The carbon range starts at $2,400 with the Tiagra SL 4. The SLR 9 AXS 2x I tested costs $11,499.

Trek also offers an ultralight SLR 9 AXS 1x with 28mm tires. Trek describes it as the racier interpretation of the Domane, but it did not vibration-test that configuration. If comfort is a big reason you’re considering the bike, pay attention to the tire setup, not just the frame name.

If you’re shopping for a Domane, which versions are you weighing? Would you spend more for the SLR’s lower weight and Project One options, or put that money toward another bike or gear?

According to recent reports, trek says it applied aero lessons from the Gen 8 Madone, but aerodynamics weren’t a major priority. In a pedaling-mannequin test, Trek claims the Gen 5 improved by 0.6 watts over Gen 4.

In other words, essentially the same.

It has been revealed that that seems appropriate. Trek prioritized weight, simplicity, and ride quality instead of chasing another aero headline.

The fifth-generation Domane is an excellent road bike. It’s light, comfortable, stable, and lively. It’s easier to adjust and service than many integrated performance bikes, retains useful mounts, and drops features that added weight and complexity without improving the bike enough to justify them.

In a recent development, the old Domanes were more technically adventurous. I miss that part of the story more than I miss riding them.

For most riders, I think Gen 5 is the right Trek road bike. The SL 6 AXS is the model I’d point people toward first. The SLR makes sense if you want the lighter frame and factory customization, but the expensive build doesn’t change the core experience. Taken as a whole, the new Domane is my favorite drop-bar bike Trek makes.

According to recent reports, that’s my take after riding the bike. Now I want to hear from people who own a Domane, have ridden an earlier version, or are considering the Gen 5. What questions do you still have? What would you like me to investigate or compare? I’ll continue the conversation on Discord and bring the most useful questions and experiences back here.

According to recent reports, what do you think of the upcoming Trek Domane? What questions do you still have? What did I screw up? If you own or have ridden the Gen 5 Domane, share your impressions.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Latest Update: No Alps, No Pyrenees, and No Paris. The 2027 Tour de France Femmes Will Still Deliver Exciting Racing, but the Women Deserve More of Cycling’s Iconic Backdrops.

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The route of the 2027 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift was revealed in late October, featuring a Grand Départ in the UK, a jaunt through central France, and a summit finish atop the Puy de Dôme.
  • In just five editions, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift has become the pinnacle of the women’s WorldTour calendar.
  • Now, I don’t doubt that the women’s peloton will make the most of the route it’s given, but whether it’ll match the spectacle of previous editions is another question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The route of the 2027 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift was revealed in late October, featuring a Grand Départ in the UK, a jaunt through central France, and a summit finish atop the Puy de Dôme. The sixth edition of the revived women’s Tour will kick off on Friday, July 30, and conclude on Saturday, August 7, after nine days of racing.

In just five editions, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift has become the pinnacle of the women’s WorldTour calendar. And looking at the 2027 route, we’re in for another nine days of aggressive racing, a hard-fought GC battle, and opportunities for a wide range of stage winners. Yet some route choices leave me lukewarm, and a few things are missing altogether. There’s no trek into the Alps or Pyrenees, no individual time trial, and still no Paris finale.

Now, I don’t doubt that the women’s peloton will make the most of the route it’s given, but whether it’ll match the spectacle of previous editions is another question.

First, the highlights, starting with the three-day Grand Départ in England.

The 2027 route puts a lot of the fireworks up front, so there’s no easing into this Tour. It opens with a short, punchy 86km stage from Leeds to Manchester. Officially classified as flat, it still packs in three categorized climbs. So while the sprinters may get their chance at the first yellow jersey, it’s not guaranteed. Then comes a bumpy stage two that, a local tells me, is much harder on the legs than it looks on paper. And then we’ll get the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift’s first team time trial in London.

Leeds, Manchester, London. The 2027 edition will put women’s racing in front of millions. That’s a huge opportunity to draw roadside crowds and reach upcoming audiences. Those opening stages could also give the GC an intriguing shape. An early winner backed by a strong team performance in London might carry a rider in yellow deep into the race.

Industry observers note that then there’s the Puy de Dôme. The volcano occupies a special place in cycling history, having hosted 14 men’s Tour de France stage finishes, including the famous 1964 head-to-head between Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor.

A more recent memory of the Puy de Dôme is that of Matteo Jorgenson’s heartbreak on stage nine of the 2023 Tour. The American attacked alone with almost 50km remaining, only for Canadian Michael Woods to catch and pass him some 450 meters from victory. Jorgenson ultimately finished fourth.

It’s easy to imagine the volcano hosting another exciting chapter in the Kasia Niewiadoma (Canyon//SRAM) and Demi Vollering (FDJ United–Suez) rivalry.

According to recent reports, in 2025, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift delivered six different stage winners and three riders in yellow. This year, it was six and five respectively. The 2027 route should again give a broad cast of riders their chance, with plenty of terrain for versatile stage hunters alongside opportunities for the sprinters and climbers.

That’s something I like about the Tour. A Tour stage can define a rider’s season; just look at the breakthrough victories of Maëva Squiban (UAE Team L'Imad), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education–Oatly), and Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance–Soudal) in years past.

The route opens the door to well-rounded riders, but the overall will still likely be decided on the final two mountainous days. But if climbing decides the Tour, I’d like to see some high-mountain racing in the Alps or Pyrenees. If the intention is to give more riders a shot at the GC, then I want to believe that they can actually take the yellow home, rather than just borrow it for a few days.

According to recent reports, of course, Vollering and Niewiadoma excel on punchy terrain too. And that’s part of my concern: different profiles don’t guarantee different outcomes. Perhaps the shorter climbs will keep more riders in contention, but I’m not convinced this route broadens the fight for yellow as much as it prolongs it.

Then there’s London. I’m excited about the setting, but the racing format leaves me underwhelmed. I prefer an individual time trial where every rider controls her own performance. No matter the timing rules, a team time trial tends to favor stronger, bigger teams, with more money to spend on a deeper roster, equipment, testing, and optimizing. A rider from a team with fewer resources could leave London with a time loss that reflects her team's budget more than her own performance.

Eighteen kilometers may limit the damage, but as 2024 indicated, when Niewiadoma-Phinney won the overall by just four seconds, every single second counts.

While Britain gets the big-city showcases, I feel roadside fans in France get a bad deal. The route bypasses the country’s largest cities on its way to a finale where spectator access remains uncertain.

Strict environmental protections are in place on Puy de Dôme, and organizers are still exploring if they can admit a limited crowd at the summit. I understand the need for protection, but a repeat of 2023’s empty upper slopes would be a lonely way to welcome in the Tour winner. If fans aren’t welcome, surely it’s worth asking whether this is the right place to finish.

And while a summit finish can deliver exciting racing, I’m still waiting to see the women’s peloton finish on the cobblestones of Paris, same as the men. Wout van Aert’s victory in 2025 and Mathieu van der Poel’s all-out effort in 2026 were absolute highlights of those Tours for me. The Montmartre circuit has shown how much racing in Paris can offer, beyond a ceremonial procession. After watching Vollering and Niewiadoma duel in France and again in Montréal, with Marlen Reusser never far behind, I want to see what these women could do on those streets.

Latest Update: Isakova and Hidalgo Win Final WTCS Races in Abu Dhabi, Jorgensen Podiums

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is presently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour.
  • Industry observers note that the top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent.
  • 2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the significant name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Wagner Araujo/World Triathlon).

The postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is presently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

Industry observers note that the top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the significant name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

In a recent development, isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would rapidly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

In a recent development, halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

At the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

According to recent reports, by halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

That momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”.

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

In the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of new world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

Newly introduced Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other major name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

It started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

In a recent development, wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

Recent findings suggest that almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

According to recent reports, perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and company. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the major question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

Onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde quickly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

Sources indicate that the front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He rapidly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

It was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”.

Wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his dominant T100 season.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Build your balance in Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou Points. All three transfer 1:1 to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. A combination of signup bonuses and regular spend can reach this in 3-6 months.

It has been revealed that ANA releases partner award space 331 days before departure. Mark your target date and search United.com (which highlights Star Alliance partner availability) or ANA.com to confirm business class seats exist before transferring any points.

Once you confirm availability, transfer your points to your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account. Chase and Amex transfers are typically instant. Do not transfer speculatively. Only move points when you see the seat.

Sources indicate that partner award bookings must be made by phone. Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at their US number. Have your dates, route, and membership number ready. The agent will process the booking and confirm your seat assignment.

Verify your flight is on a Boeing 777-300ER, which is the aircraft with "The Room" product. Check your confirmation on ANA.com and monitor for any equipment changes closer to departure.

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from Fresh York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. ⁠Before You Spend on Gravel Suspension, Try Wider Tubeless Tires for a Simpler, Smoother Ride

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively new gravel bike.
  • In a recent development, when I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

It has been revealed that just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively new gravel bike. He was considering different suspension components as a means to gain comfort while he rides—especially on chunkier gravel. He mentioned his frame isn’t compatible with a suspension fork, but was looking at parts like a suspension stem and suspension seatpost. If this sounds like you read this before hitting add to cart on those parts.

In a recent development, when I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike. Certain riders fit the bill for a suspension seat post or suspension stem. A few customers had prostate challenges and a suspension seat post helped them stay on the bike longer. Others had wrist or hand issues and they benefited from a suspension stem. But even those riders could get additional comfort from a simple change.

After trying all the suspension components I could add to my own bike (as well as trying a full-suspension gravel bike), I have realized that throwing suspension at a gravel bike doesn’t necessarily fix the issue of being more comfortable on the ride. In the shop, customers would ask about installing a suspension fork on a hybrid or gravel bike, but not all frames are even compatible with a suspension fork.

Industry observers note that adding suspension parts to the bike can change the overall feel of the bike, not to mention the weight those parts typically add. When riders are looking for more comfort on their gravel bike the component swap I pick first is simple—wider tires. Here we’ll talk about the benefits of wider tires and why going tubeless gives your ride that extra bit of cush.

Step one of getting more comfortable on your gravel bike is setting up your tires as tubeless if they aren’t already set up that way. Tubeless systems allow you to run your pressure lower compared to running tubes, which in combination with a wider tire offers more comfort. Running tubes with a lower tire pressure leaves you susceptible to pinch flats, but tubeless systems remove the tubes from the equation.

One easy way to check if your tires are set up as tubeless is to loosen the nut at the bottom of your valve and gently press it into the rim. If you press it in and air starts to come out, then tighten the nut back up—congratulations, your tires are set up as tubeless!

If they aren’t tubeless, then it’s time to check compatibility. Check the specs of your bike to see if your rim and tire are tubeless-compatible. If they aren’t you’ll have to explore fresh wheel and tire options, but if they’re compatible you can convert them to tubeless. Some bikes come stock with tubeless-compatible rims and tires, but don’t come set up tubeless out of the box. Tubeless systems require specific rim tape or rim strips to properly set them up. I’ve seen plenty of bikes come with tubes installed, but with rims taped with tubeless tape. Again, check your individual bike’s specs to see if this includes your bike.

It has been revealed that if you need to pull the tubes out of your tubeless-compatible wheels and tires, then you’ll need a few things. First is a good set of tubeless valves. My favorite are Muc-Off Tubeless Valves. They come with a valve core remover tool on the valve cap, come in different lengths depending on your rim depth, and there are a myriad of colors to add a little pop to your bike. You’ll also need tubeless sealant. I’ve tested more sealants than I can remember, but the tried-and-true sealant I go back to is Stan’s Sealant. Tara Seplavy, Bicycling’s Deputy Editor, walks through setting up your tubeless tires here.

Recent findings suggest that A bike rarely comes stock with the widest tire that fits in the bike. For example, the Trek Checkpoint SL5 is equipped with 700x42mm, but can fit up to 700x50mm tires when there are no fenders on the bike. Always check the technical specifications for your specific make and model to see how wide you can go. Over the last few years, bike manufacturers have been pushing the envelope to allow for wider and wider tires on bikes. If you have a previous model-year bike that doesn’t mean you can bank on the current model’s tire clearance fitting your bike. Be sure to check the correct generation for your specific make and model. If you go with a tire wider than the maximum width for your bike, you risk damaging the fork and frame.

It has been revealed that on my own gravel rig, I recently bumped from 700x40mm tires to 700x45mm tires and noticed the difference immediately. I stuck with the same tire make and model—the Pirelli Cinturato H. The extra five millimeters of width immediately gave more comfort and traction on chunkier gravel and some local singletrack; even with the same tire tread. Five millimeters might not sound like a lot, but it added significant comfort while putting out rides longer than one hundred miles.

Wider tires are the right choice for many—even if you aren’t pushing your mileage into the triple digits. Recently I bumped up the tire width on my dad’s gravel bike. Adding wider tires to his bike (as well as a slightly thicker handlebar tape) leveled up his comfort level while riding. Whether you are taking your gravel bike on singletrack, chunky gravel, hundred-mile rides, or just want a little more comfort on your local lunch loop, go tubeless and bump up your tire width.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

The 3 Types of Running Workouts You Need to Train for Your First Half Marathon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that nowhere in any running rulebook does it say you have to train for a 5K or 10K before signing up for a half marathon.
  • Cut to Runner’s World’s 20-week beginner half marathon plan created by Meg Takacs, CPT, a UESCA-certified running coach and founder of the Movement and Miles app.
  • In a recent development, it balances three key workouts designed to help you build endurance safely, recover well, and get comfortable with longer distances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that nowhere in any running rulebook does it say you have to train for a 5K or 10K before signing up for a half marathon. As a beginner, 13.1 miles is an awesome way to approach long-distance running. You just need a plan that meets you where you’re at right now and progresses gradually to get you to the starting line feeling strong.

Cut to Runner’s World’s 20-week beginner half marathon plan created by Meg Takacs, CPT, a UESCA-certified running coach and founder of the Movement and Miles app.

In a recent development, it balances three key workouts designed to help you build endurance safely, recover well, and get comfortable with longer distances. You’ll spread these workouts throughout 20 weeks, which gives you plenty of time to build rather than your typical 10- or 14-week plan.

Each workout progresses as you move through the plan, so it’s a good idea to familiarize yourself with their basic structure and purpose before you jump into training. Here’s how to get the most out of each workout.

DOWNLOAD YOUR ZERO TO HALF PLAN HERE.

According to recent reports, run/walks help you build aerobic fitness and endurance gradually. You’ll start with a one-minute run followed by a one-minute walk for 20 minutes total, adding one minute to the run interval every session. With run/walks starting at three times a week, you’ll work up to a 10-mile run/walk in week 16, where you run for 20-minute intervals and walk for two minutes (this is your weekend long run).

Industry observers note that do the run intervals at a comfortable, low-intensity pace, meaning you should be able to hold a conversation with a friend the whole time. On a scale of 1 to 10 for rate of perceived exertion (RPE), aim for a 2 to 4 for effort level, with 1 being easy like a walk and 10 meaning all-out effort.

Sources indicate that why it works: This is the backbone of the beginner half marathon initiative. Run/walk sessions help you build the endurance you need to run farther.

10 x 1 minute walk, 1 minute easy-effort run.

Sources indicate that in week four of this initiative, you’ll start incorporating continuous easy runs, beginning with 25 minutes at a truly easy effort. The longest continuous run you will complete is 8 miles with as few walk breaks as possible by week 17.

Throughout the blueprint, there’s more of a focus on time-based easy runs rather than distance. “For beginners, time on your feet is more important than mileage in order to get your body gradually acclimated to running,” Takacs previously told Runner’s World.

Why it works: Continuous easy runs help boost endurance and give you the confidence you need to run farther.

Run 25 minutes at an easy effort (RPE 2 to 4), limiting walk breaks as much as possible.

The first of your weekly speed workouts begins in week 3. You’ll complete 400-meter repeats at a moderate effort with two-minute walks in between. Moderate effort is slightly above your easy effort, reaching a 4 to 6 out of 10 RPE. “The goal is to try and run each repeat faster than the last,” Takacs adds.

Sources indicate that you should still be able to speak during the work intervals, but you’re breathing heavier and can only talk in phrases. Over the course of the training strategy, you’ll work your way up to longer intervals, like 800-meter, 1200-meter, and mile repeats.

Why it works: Speed workouts aren’t just there to help you get faster; they also boost your overall fitness and running economy so easy runs feel easier.

Recent findings suggest that short postrun strides help build speed and leg turnover, and you’ll find them sprinkled throughout your initiative. These accelerations will help you build more speed, improve your running form by getting your legs to turn over quicker, and boost your confidence.

According to recent reports, the goal of strides is to run at a hard effort for 10 to 15 seconds, but it doesn’t have to be an all-out sprint. Aim for a 7 to 10 RPE; you should only be able to say a word or three at a time.

In any training initiative, strength workouts are crucial to prevent injury, support your running economy and durability, and get stronger. In this plan, you’ll complete strength workouts once or twice a week before or after your runs. Depending on your preference, you can decide to run in the morning, then follow with strength in the afternoon or evening (or vice versa).

Takacs recommends starting with bodyweight exercises if you’re new to strength training and then adding in weights as you get stronger.

GET 30-MIN STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

In a recent development, there’s a reason coaches tell runners to work hard and recover harder. Your recovery days are meant to feel like a true recovery where you can come back to your next run feeling refreshed, strong, and excited to get back out there.

It’s a good idea to loosen stiff muscles with foam rolling, stretching, and some mobility drills. If you need a complete day off, it’s also okay to not do anything at all except watch TV, read a book, or hang out with friends. A day off is good for the mind and the body. This is also a good opportunity to make sure you’re getting to bed early so you can show up to each run as your best, well-rested self.

In a recent development, kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and right now competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when a rider switches from flat pedals to clipless pedals, they typically aren’t thinking about the differences of pedals like Shimano SPD or SPD-SL, Wahoo Speedplays, or egg-beater pedals. Many times, they haven’t heard of Time pedals or the different Assioma or Garmin models. The first thought many have is, “How do I get out of the pedal once I’m clipped in?”.

It has been revealed that not all people considering the switch realize this—as contradictory as it sounds, clipless pedals refer to a pedal system where you are clipped into the pedal. If you aren’t familiar with the system, think about being clipped into a ski binding. Some pedal options offer different release settings—similar to how a DIN setting on a ski binding can be adjusted to offer different levels of force needed to release the ski boot from the binding.

Here we’ll dig into what clipless pedals are, how they can benefit you on your ride, tips for setting up your pedals and cleats, and tips for those daunting first few rides with your newly introduced pedals.

I have plenty of friends who swear by the saying, “flat pedals win medals.” However, there is a reason you’ll only see clipless pedals at world tour road races or on the majority of gravel bikes at your local gravel grinder. When you ride clipped in you end up using more of your leg musculature during each revolution of your pedal stroke.

In short, this means you’re typically more efficient when using clipless pedals compared to flat pedals. For clarity, you don’t need to ride clipless pedals to be a cyclist. But for those riders looking to take their riding to the next level, it’s worth giving them a try.

Because you’re literally attached to the pedal, you use not only your quads in the downstroke part of the revolution, but you also work your hamstrings, hip flexors, and glutes as you pull up. All of those muscles at work translate to more power while you’re riding, especially as you refine your pedaling technique. To get started, here’s your expert-backed guide to pedaling with clipless pedals—without falling over.

According to recent reports, “Cleat placement is paramount,” indicates Issac Denham, owner of bike fitting studio Befitting Bicycles in Wayne, Pennsylvania. “Since incorrect cleat placement can lead to injuries, we suggest booking time with a bike fitter to place your cleats. Having a professional install your cleats also ensures that they won’t be installed improperly or even upside down.”.

Sources indicate that for those riders that want to try clipless pedals, but don’t want to jump into a precision fit, start with cleats in a neutral position. This means setting the cleats up in the middle of the slots in the shoe with the cleats relatively straight. Just make sure the left and right cleats are in roughly the same position—this will give you a good baseline moving forward.

It will take time doing the guess and check method for cleat placement, but this method gives you the chance to play around going clipless before you invest hundreds into a bike fit. If you start to develop pain after using clipless pedals, stop pedaling. This is likely due to cleat position and that is when it is time to see a local trusted shop for direction.

According to recent reports, “Many clipless pedals have adjustable pedal tension. This is basically how hard the built-in spring holds the cleat in the pedal,” says Dan Chabonov, Bicycling test editor. “Setting this tension as low as possible means you need less force to clip in and out of the pedals and can make the learning process a little easier.”.

While most clipless pedals already come set at the lowest tension setting from the manufacturer, you can also easily make the adjustment.

In a recent development, “Typically out of the box, pedals are set up with the least amount of release tension,” says Becky Quinn, former pro and bike fitter. “The pedal tensioner is on the rear of the pedal. There is a small 3mm bolt that requires a 3mm Allen wrench to adjust the tension. It can be turned counterclockwise to loosen the tension or clockwise to tighten it. There is a small window on the back of the pedal that has a small horizontal pin that moves up or down depending on which way you turn the tensioner.”.

If you adjust the tension on your pedals, make sure you confirm that the pins are in the same place on both the left and right pedal, so the release tension is the same on both sides.

Sources indicate that practice does indeed make perfect when it comes to learning how to pedal with clipless pedals. The goal is to become so comfortable with the movements that they become part of your muscle memory, so you don’t have to look down at your foot or pedal for longer than a quick glance.

When you’re just starting out pedaling with clipless pedals, do it inside first. “Practicing indoors either on a trainer, or even leaned up against a wall, can be a great place to start where you don’t have to worry about falling down or looking silly,” claims Denham.

When I ran a shop and was getting people set up on clipless pedals, I would suggest they get on the bike inside, ideally on a trainer or next to a wall to stabilize themselves, then put on a show or a movie. It sounds monotonous (and the people you live with might give you an odd look or two), but simply clip in, clip out, clip in, clip out, over and over. Do it looking down at your shoe, then when that’s comfortable practice doing it without looking down. Feel it out inside and you’ll be much better off when you head out the door.

To clip into your pedal, start with the pedal positioned at the bottom of the pedal stroke.

Industry observers note that “Softly lift the front of the pedal with your toe to flip it over so that you can engage. Your toe will be slightly pointed downward. Slide your foot forward until the tongue of the cleat stops on the lip of the pedal,” Quinn explains. “Once you can’t slide your foot any further forward, continue to pedal forward and add pressure to the pedal. It will click in. Sometimes you will need to rotate your heel inward or outward at the 6 o’clock position to engage securely.”.

In a recent development, then it’s time to clip out: “In order to practice clipping out of your pedals, place one leg all the way down to the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock). Then, firmly rotate your heel outward. Be sure to not roll your ankle,” Quinn advises. “The motion should be similar to that of smashing a bug under the ball of your foot.”.

It has been revealed that if there is a single gem of advice we would love to pass on to every cyclist who has ever learned how to ride with clipless pedals, this would be it: Unclip the foot you intend to put down when you come to a stop before you come to a stop. “This is the most important piece of the puzzle,” says Quinn.

Once you unclip, “here is the most critical piece: Keep the unclipped foot on the pedal but continue to pedal a half stroke,” Quinn adds. “Once the foot that is still clipped in gets to the 6 o’clock position, coast and stand up. Your butt needs to get off the saddle. Continue to apply your rear brakes until you are almost at a stop. When you are about to come to a complete stop, apply your front brake and step down with the unclipped foot.”.

Many cleat and pedal systems will follow a similar process with the general idea being: line up the cleat on the pedal and add downward force to clip in once the cleat is aligned.

Remember how we said switching to clipless pedals is a cycling rite of passage of sorts? Well, so is falling over as you’re learning. Practicing while riding on grass can make the falls a little easier, and falling with the proper technique (yes, there’s a technique for falling, too!) will lower your chances of serious injury.

Sources indicate that “You will fall. We all have done it and it’s okay,” notes Quinn. “Just remember that if you start to fall over, turn your buttocks so you land on it. It is the most padding we have on our bodies. Putting out an arm can break a wrist. You most likely will only get a bruise on your butt.”.

Sources indicate that the most key thing is not to get in your head, beat yourself up, or give up. Falling over at least a few times has happened to every single cyclist who rides with clipless pedals.

I’ll never forget one of my first rides with clipless pedals. I rolled over to the group in the parking lot overly confident, forgot I had to unclip my foot from the pedal, and slowly tipped over—still attached to the bike. It happens to everyone when you’re first making the switch, but some practice at home can make the transition a little less painful.

Natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

6 Tips for Maintaining Your Fitness Routine During the Busy Holiday Season

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the holiday season has arrived, and with it, plenty of reasons your fitness routine may slide.
  • Recent findings suggest that well, consider this: You don’t have to do as much as you think to maintain your fitness between now and Fresh Year’s Day.
  • Researchers also found that, in generally active adults, cutting training frequency to just twice a week for up to 15 weeks could maintain short-term endurance and VO₂ max.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the holiday season has arrived, and with it, plenty of reasons your fitness routine may slide. Between shopping for gifts, attending holiday parties, and meeting work obligations, it can feel like there’s not enough time to squeeze in an hour-long workout session—so why even try?

Recent findings suggest that well, consider this: You don’t have to do as much as you think to maintain your fitness between now and Fresh Year’s Day. A review published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021 suggests that you can reduce your workout time by two-thirds and still maintain your gains, as long as the intensity stays the same.

Researchers also found that, in generally active adults, cutting training frequency to just twice a week for up to 15 weeks could maintain short-term endurance and VO₂ max.

In a recent development, setting an attainable goal for yourself, like running for at least 30 minutes two or three times per week, can make staying active through the holidays feel more doable. It’s how I was able to get back to exercise after a break, and it’s also how I blueprint to maintain my fitness this winter—in addition to following some of the best advice from my Runner’s World colleagues.

So ditch the all-or-nothing mindset and use the following tips to your advantage now, so when the Fresh Year arrives, you’ll be ready to tackle your goals for 2027.

“I have a race in mid-January, so I am following a training strategy [which keeps me motivated]. But I am also cross-training with step aerobics, and I’ve added jump training into my workouts. I was bored with my usual strength routine, so I decided to mix things up with kettlebell training, targeting my upper body and core.” —Donna Raskin, senior health and fitness editor.

“I make time for fresh workout classes, like the ones offered by Solidcore and OrangeTheory to support my strength needs, because I usually don’t get to attend those sessions when I’m training for a race.” —Sara Hemstock, senior director of marketing and brand liaison.

“I love doing strength work and some form of speed training in the winter. I recently found an indoor track in my local YMCA, and I’m excited to use that as an option for when it snows. There’s something nostalgic about it for me after running winter track as a kid.” —Kristine Kearns, associate health and fitness editor.

“I love running on Christmas Day because it’s always so quiet in my hometown of Columbia, South Carolina. I usually run downtown, past the state capitol building, and through the University of South Carolina. The normally busy area turns into a complete ghost town! It’s a once-a-year experience and a personal tradition. I look forward to it every year.” —Theo Khaler, news editor.

“Every year, I look forward to going home to North Carolina during the holidays because I get to test my fitness in my neighborhood Turkey Trot. It’s a community event put on by my high school, and it always draws a huge crowd.

The 5K race itself gives me something to look toward and train for in the fall. It’s a great chance to test my speed and have fun with the sport, but the best part has to be the community aspect. I catch up with old friends, teammates, coaches, teachers, and neighbors, and hearing about their own running journeys always fuels mine, too. Plus, each age-group winner wins a pie. Who doesn’t like free dessert?” —Ashley Tysiac, content hype editor.

In a recent development, “I motivate myself by thinking of all the folks who decided not to run as I was bundled up, gutting out a sub-freezing effort. It just makes me feel proud thinking that I decided to lace up and get out the door that particular day when someone else may not have.

The thought process works both ways: If I decide to skip a cold-weather run, I think about all the people who are out there toughing it out while I’m sipping hot chocolate on my couch.” —Matt Rudisill, associate service editor.

“This is the time of year when I try to add strength work into my routine because I am usually indoors at the gym more. But I find strength training so boring, so I experiment with different protein shakes to find the ones I really like, which keeps me motivated. I consider them a postworkout treat!” —Amanda Furrer, running reviews editor.

“I treat myself to nice, latest running clothes, and that makes cold weather running more enjoyable. I also like testing out new looks. It gives me something to look forward to.”—Hemstock.

Industry observers note that “Indoor workouts allow me to experiment with different outfits, like a shirt with comfortable sweatpants or oversized sweatsuits. That makes me feel really cozy and confident so I want to keep on training.” —Kearns.

Sources indicate that “I try to run at least a mile every day through the holidays, like a running streak. It can be inside or outside.” —Furrer.

“I give myself permission to shorten any and all workouts. Even if I just commit to 20 minutes, I usually end up doing more, but knowing I can stop early breaks down the barrier to getting started.” —Mallory Creveling, deputy editor, health and fitness.

Sources indicate that monique LeBrun is a health and fitness editor who is based in Easton, Pennsylvania. She covers a wide range of health and wellness topics, with a primary focus on running performance and nutrition. Monique is passionate about creating content that empowers runners to become the best versions of themselves. As an avid runner and parent, she loves spending time outdoors with her daughter, who often accompanies her on weekend runs as her personal mini run coach.

#137027. Both Men and Women Are Quitting Running Because of Undiagnosed Pelvic Floor Problems. Experts Want to Break the Taboo So More Runners Can Get Help.

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3427 w)
