Sources indicate that bike lights are a must-have item for anyone commuting or riding road or gravel in the winter months. Even if you already have a light, I’ve found it super useful to own an extra set to have at the office, on my other bikes, or as spares for friends.

Lezyne consistently makes great front and rear lights. While slightly pricier than budget picks found on Amazon or AliExpress, they’re durable, work well, and last several seasons. Plus, we’ve found Lezyne’s advertised runtimes and lumens are much closer to reality than many no-name lights.

According to recent reports, showers Pass makes our best-tested winter gloves, and they’re at the moment on sale at 19% off. In their review, our test rider said, “This knit, waterproof glove has a midweight feel and sufficient insulation when temperatures hover around freezing. Most riders will find the Crosspoints reach its limit at about 30-35 degrees, depending on how hard you’re riding.”.

It has been revealed that the glove traps some body heat, so your fingers may be slightly chilly at first but will warm up within 15 minutes. Better yet, when the mercury climbs, your hands won’t feel hot and sweaty.

Recent findings suggest that electric mini-inflators burst onto the scene a couple of years ago and have rapidly become a rider favorite for pumping up your tires at home, at the trailhead, or on rides. Of the inflators we’ve tested, the RockBros model stands out for its consistency and is a favorite of Bicycling editors. It’s compact, lightweight, and has an accurate gauge. In our testing of 15 electric pumps, it inflated a road tire to 65 psi in 45 seconds, and filled five tires before running out of power.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2—Bicycling’s Best Overall Indoor Trainer—is on sale for the lowest price we’ve seen: $399.99. The Core combines excellent performance, great accuracy, and high max resistance in a package perfect for Zwift rides after work, winter training, and even competitive virtual racing.

Sources indicate that indoor training bikes are quickly gaining popularity for their ease of use and low maintenance. With a dedicated indoor setup, you no longer have to wrestle with getting your bike on or off the smart trainer, which also makes it convenient to share with other riders in your family. Plus, you won’t wear out pricey parts. Zwift’s Ride is our favorite: it sets up quickly and adjusts for a wide range of rider heights and fits. It also costs thousands less than its competitors.

Shorter daylight hours and lower temps often mean fewer hours spent riding outside on the road or trail. An indoor trainer helps you maintain your fitness through the winter months while getting your riding fix. Garmin’s Tacx Flux2 is the brand’s mid-range smart trainer; with 2,000 watts of resistance, it simulates gradients up to 16%. The Flux also connects to virtual platforms like Zwift and Rouvy for immersive indoor riding experiences.

Sources indicate that stainless bottles have become popular among cyclists over the past several seasons. They keep water chilled on hot rides and don’t give your water a funny plastic taste. Many gravel and off-road riders love CamelBak’s Stainless Podium, particularly for its open/closed twist-lock cap. The Podium Stainless also ranked best in our heat testing last summer and performed well in our winter bottle testing.

SUMMER BOTTLE TESTING WINTER BOTTLE TESTING.

Elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price.

Weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs significantly less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

Sources indicate that this helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis uses the Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

In a recent development, MET’s Trenta 3K Carbon is one of the top five road helmets by Virginia Tech’s helmet lab. It’s also one of the best for racing and high-performance riding, as proven by UAE Team Emirates’s results—Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Industry observers note that unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. Typically priced over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit, but this deal cuts the cost by almost a third.

Arm warmers are among the most versatile pieces of cycling clothing you can own. This magical piece of kit turns your short-sleeve jersey into a long-sleeve in seconds—and you can change back to short sleeves again mid-ride if the temps rise.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve owned many pairs of arm warmers over the last three decades, and I rarely ride without them on my arms or in my jersey pocket if the temperatures are between 45 and 60 degrees. Castelli makes some of the best clothes out there, and these arm warmers are a steal for the price. They’re easy to pull on or off while riding, and they don’t sag.

It has been revealed that A quality rain jacket is a must-have item for riders who live anywhere it rains or snows. Rapha’s Core Rain Jacket is great option for layering over your winter jersey without adding too much bulk. It features a two-way zip for regulating body temperature, reflective hits for riding after dusk or in the early morning, and packs down small if weather clears mid-ride.

Industry observers note that if you ride in temps below 40 degrees, a good cycling jacket is a great asset. As a Scottish brand, Endura knows a few things about riding in the cold, dark days of winter, and its MT500 Freezing Point jacket is a great option for trail rides and commuting in low temps. It features PrimaLoft Gold insulation and a DWR finish to shed rain drops. Another great feature is the MT500’s underarm zippers; they allow you to cool off and ventilate without unzipping your entire jacket.

Recent findings suggest that when cold weather hits, bib tights ensure you stay warm on rides. Of the many cycling tights available, Velocio makes some of our test editors’ favorites. The One Thermal bibs feature a soft, fleece lining and use a more relaxed, less compressive fit than some of the brands’ other options. This makes them perfect for road, gravel, and trail rides, or even layering under commuter pants.

Instead of shredding your nice, lightweight road tires on weather-worn winter roads, swap them out for more durable rubber. Vittoria’s Rubino tires are a proven all-season road tire with a smooth, fast-rolling center and siped edges for cornering traction. They’re tubeless-compatible, so you’ll catch fewer flats in the cold, and come in widths from 26mm to 34mm with black or tan sidewalls.

Modern bike computers do much more than display speed and distance. These devices are a critical information hub for many cyclists. Cycling computers can record ride metrics, display real-time performance data, and help you navigate—but that’s only scratching the surface of their capabilities.

It has been revealed that the Elemnt Bolt 3 is Wahoo’s tiny-but-mighty cycling-specific computer. Wahoo equips it with a 2.3-inch high-resolution screen, up to 20 hours of battery life, and integration with Strava, Komoot, and other popular cycling platforms.

In a recent development, another great option is the Hammerhead Karoo. This head unit features a 3.2-inch color touchscreen Gorilla Glass display and up to 35 hours of run time. The Karoo stands out for its mapping and navigation. The navigation, combined with its pop-up hill climb feature and ability to sideload apps, makes the Karoo my overall favorite.

POC makes comfortable, well-ventilated helmets for road, gravel, and mountain biking. The Kortal is a trail-style helmet, featuring an adjustable visor, room to stow your glasses or goggles, and plenty of airflow for hot summer trail rides. The straps are also comfortable, something that often bugs me on other lids.

Fresh bar tape is the quickest and most cost-effective way to improve the look, feel, and comfort of any road or gravel bike. I’ve used Fizik tape on several bikes that have come in for testing, and have also bought it for my personal bikes. It has enough cushion, reliable grip, and is easy to wrap. You can’t ask for much more from bar tape.

Industry observers note that while many riders are adding electric mini-inflators to their tool kits, a quality floor pump remains an essential part of every cyclist’s arsenal. They never run out of batteries, pump as many tires as your arms can handle, and are easy to use.

Riders and mechanics have trusted Topeak’s JoeBlow pumps for decades—because they work. Although many JoeBlow models are low-cost and utilitarian, the JoeBlow Ace DX is a Cadillac-level floor pump. It features alloy construction with a metal chuck and can inflate tires up to 260 psi, with three different inflation modes: high-volume, standard, or high-pressure.

Is Your AI Strength Strategy Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.
  • Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.
  • We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day blueprint complete with sets and reps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete).

It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.

Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.

We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day blueprint complete with sets and reps.

Day one covered the lower body and core: squats or goblet squats, Romanian deadlifts, reverse lunges, standing calf raises, dead bugs, and side planks.

Day two went after the upper body and posterior chain: dumbbell bench press or push-ups, rows, lat pulldowns or assisted pull-ups, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, glute bridges or hip thrusts, and Pallof presses. The prescription included three sets of 8-10 reps, for 40 to 50 minutes per session, to be followed for 8-12 weeks.

Sources indicate that it all looked perfectly sensible and not too dissimilar to what many triathletes do in most strength workouts. But for a triathlete who’s already squeezing three sports into one week, strength workouts should really be periodized and designed to augment what’s happening in the triathlete’s sport-specific training life (and the off-season is the one time of year when it’s great to do more in the gym, not less).

So with this in mind, we handed the plan to strength coach Sam Hengehold, who works with triathletes of all ages and abilities at Kinesis Integrated Performance in Boulder, Colorado. “I’d argue it is not right, but it’s also not wrong,” she states. “The plan is general, but it is not beneficial.”.

Here’s the surprise: Hengehold wouldn’t strike a single exercise from the list.

“All exercises listed are actually great and could very well be integrated into a triathlete strength routine,” she indicates. “The limiter here is the lack of periodization and volume/load variables.”.

Two of ChatGPT’s picks earn special praise:.

Calf raises: “Many triathletes miss this integral exercise in their strength routine,” Hengehold says. “Lower leg injuries are extremely common with triathletes.” As a general rule, Hengehold wants athletes working toward calf raises at 1.5 times their body weight to build resiliency against injury in the calf, ankle, and foot.

Industry observers note that glute bridges: “A safe way to build power for beginners in strength training,” Hengehold indicates. They mostly train the glutes and core, the muscle groups that underpin all three disciplines.

So if the exercises are fine, where does the wasted time come in? It’s in how the initiative asks you to do them.

To its credit, ChatGPT suggests lifting less often as race day approaches and adding a little load once the sets feel solid. But the exercises, sets, and reps never change. Your swim, bike, and run training is built in cycles around your races, and Hengehold advises that your lifting should be too.

Sources indicate that in the off-season, strength work can take priority and endurance training becomes the base. In race season, that flips: Lifting is there to support your swim, bike, and run, and to keep your body resilient. A blueprint that looks identical in January and July does neither job well.

“Over time, it will just be an energy suck of a session, causing more fatigue in the athlete with minimal benefit,” Hengehold warns.

Industry observers note that chatGPT’s warm-up gets one line: 5-10 minutes of easy cardio, mobility, and lighter practice sets. Hengehold wants something more deliberate, with activation work chosen to prepare you for the main lift of the day.

Sources indicate that “Warm-up and activation encourages proper form and oils the muscles,” Hengehold says. “Typically, that would include some sort of dynamic stretching, mobility, or preparation exercise that will aid in the main lift goals of the session. Before squats, for example, that might mean 90/90 hip rotations for hip mobility and banded clamshells to wake up the gluteus medius.” This matters if you want to avoid injury and get the most from every rep.

Recent findings suggest that the major, complex lifts belong at the start of the session, when you’re fresh and can control your form. They also work better when paired with an athletic movement, Hengehold notes, so the brain learns what the strength is for.

Follow loaded squats with box jumps, for instance, and you reinforce the power you need at toe-off on the run or when pushing watts on the bike. ChatGPT’s plan has no jumps and no explosive work at all.

“Neuromuscular understanding and adaptation is absolutely necessary for triathletes to maximize the benefit of strength training,” Hengehold states. Without it, you get some injury prevention and extra muscle mass, but not much else.

Hengehold named three categories of strength work that matter most for triathletes:.

Industry observers note that core work: Think isometric holds and slow, controlled movements, with deep breathing throughout, to work the transverse abdominal muscles. Hengehold’s picks: planks with alternating shoulder taps, dead bugs, and bird dogs.

Industry observers note that unilateral movements: Single-leg Romanian deadlifts, Bulgarian split squats, front-foot elevated reverse lunges, and single-leg calf raises all make each side do its own share of the work. Swimming, biking, and running give a stronger side plenty of chances to cover for a weaker one, and these exercises help break those overcompensation patterns.

Squat variations: Isometric squats (holding the position) and eccentric squats (slowing the lowering phase) are a safe way to build resilience in the lower body and core. The squat is also endlessly adjustable, so it can be tweaked to target whatever you need most.

What you lift, and how, should depend on how far you are from your next race.

Far from race day: This is the time for heavy strength training alongside base swim, bike, and run work. Make complex lifts the centerpiece. Hengehold likes the trap bar deadlift. Get the form and technique down first, then spend a block (typically four to six weeks) building a base with high reps and low weight. Take a deload week, then switch to low reps and heavy weight to build real strength and durability.

According to recent reports, in race season: Triathlon training takes over, and strength work drops to maintenance. Unilateral exercises move to the front, scheduled closely around your key sessions and races. Reps and load should go mostly on perceived effort and how you’re feeling, physically and emotionally. Hengehold also stresses mobility work, foam rolling, and stretching during this period.

It has been revealed that one last thing no chatbot can do is look at your form. If you’re newly introduced to the weight room, Hengehold recommends having a gym friend or personal trainer check your technique early on: “Bad habits are hard to break and cause damage over time, and the same is true with your swimming, biking, and running.”.

Yet technique is only part of what a generic blueprint misses.

“Triathletes are some of the most hardworking individuals on the planet and managing training, fatigue, and recovery requires extreme attention to detail,” Hengehold claims. “The time, energy, and hard work need to be maximized to be worth it, which means a generalized strength initiative will not meet the standard. Each athlete is a unique individual with individual needs that require an individualized plan.”.

According to recent reports, none of this is an argument against strength training — far from it. Hengehold calls it “absolutely essential to longevity in sport and health” and recommends it for every athlete. The argument is against spending your limited time and energy on a plan that wasn’t written with you in mind.

There’s something romantic about the idea of a daily run. It’s simple. It’s gritty. It’s giving “I can do hard things just because I believe I can,” main character energy. Plus, running three miles a day has become a bit of a fitness trend lately—just scroll through TikTok and you’ll see thousands of people sticking to that sweet-spot distance to get in shape, clear their heads, or just establish a healthy daily habit.

According to recent reports, I’ve dabbled in running over the years (mostly during half-hearted attempts to train for a 10K or half marathon), but I’ve never been consistent. So I challenged myself: Run (at least) three miles a day, every day, for three weeks—no skips. I wanted to see if this simple habit could actually deliver real results: Physically. Mentally. Emotionally. To cut to the chase, it did.

It has been revealed that but before we dive into exactly what I learned, here’s what the challenge I set out for actually entailed: Each day, I carved out 30-ish minutes to run a minimum of three miles—sometimes on the treadmill, sometimes outside, depending on my mood (and the weather). Sometimes fast, sometimes slow—I wasn’t chasing speed, just consistency.

And while it started out as a little personal experiment, it turned into a full-on mindset shift that seeped into other areas of my life.

Sources indicate that I’m a pretty high-energy person, even on little sleep. And frankly, when I’m not exerting that physical energy enough during the day, I find it tough to settle down to sleep at night.

Sources indicate that by week two of this challenge, I was zonking out faster than usual and waking up feeling more rested. Research backs this up—moderate aerobic exercise like running can help you fall asleep quicker and improve sleep quality, per the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine.

In a recent development, there’s a reason running is considered a moving meditation (and I say this as someone who really struggles with stationary meditating). That ~30-minute mental break from work, life, communications, etc., helped me carve out time to shut off my brain and come back to reality with a fresh outlook.

Whatever I was stressing about before my run felt way less burdensome after taking time to move my body and just, well, not stress over that thing. I’d come back with more patience, more solutions, and frankly, a more can-do attitude about dealing with whatever was weighing me down before. My run became my reset button—and a way to make myself less irritable and more focused.

In a recent development, I’ve always gained (and lost) muscle pretty promptly after starting or stopping a new exercise routine, however I typically first notice it around my abs and arms, as I'm leaner in those regions. So, when I saw my calves and quads popping a bit more in the mirror, and climbing the four flights of stairs up to my apartment started feeling easier than it used to, I knew my body was adapting. Even though I wasn’t lifting weights during this three week challenge (I tried to at first, but decided it was too much for my schedule while also running three miles daily), the repeated use of lower-body muscles while running led to strength gains.

It has been revealed that going into this challenge, I expected a mental impact of some sort (though I wasn’t quite sure what it would be), but I didn’t think my body would change much from a short-distance, short-term running habit. I already work out often (switching it up with two to three weekly strength training sessions, yoga/pilates once per week, and a two to five mile run once per week), so I didn’t think this challenge would have a palpable physical effect on me. So, the lower body muscle and strength gains were by far the most surprising benefit I walked away with.

Recent findings suggest that I’d never really consider myself a “runner,” but doing it daily for three weeks made the act feel less intimidating and more second nature to me. A study in Psychology of Sport and Exercise demonstrates that consistency in movement creates more positive attitudes toward the habit, which makes you more likely to keep showing up. My experience totally backed that up.

Sources indicate that around day six, I felt myself gearing up for my run more instinctually—getting dressed, grabbing my headphones, keys, and lacing up my sneakers just right without having to think about it much. If on the first few runs I was moseying around the neighborhood walking for several blocks to put off actually starting the run, by week two I was excitedly hitting the pavement at my three-mile pace almost as soon as I got outside. Pacing myself began to feel more natural without checking my Nike Run Club app, and I started tapping into the sound of my feet hitting the concrete to gauge my effort.

According to recent reports, before this challenge, I had a habit of engaging in pretty critical self-talk on the regular. Also, mentally checking out mid-run was the norm in order to just get through it. My internal monologue when running used to be all about how much time was left, how uncomfortable I felt, or how nice it would feel to just stop. But sticking to a daily running habit triggered the kind of awareness and shift of self-talk that I’d been long overdue for. That mindset shift was probably the biggest win of all.

In a recent development, after a few days of three miles under my belt, I started celebrating tiny wins—like not stopping on a hill or picking up my pace on the final stretch. Instead of counting down the minutes or fixating on how slow I was moving, I was hyping myself up, which only propelled me further. Whether it was a solo sunset jog or a playlist-powered treadmill sesh, I always felt a little lighter—and a little more capable of not just enduring, but thriving through hard things—post-run. That energy and positive shift in self-talk started showing up in how I talked to myself outside of workouts, too.

It’s wild how one habit tends to have a domino effect, whether it’s constructive or destructive. Once I started running every day, I realized I wanted to support that effort outside of my run window. That meant reaching for water instead of a second coffee, getting in some light stretching at night, prioritizing protein in my meals, and actually winding down for sleep earlier than usual instead of binge-watching or doom-scrolling.

The momentum from running made other wellness choices feel less like chores and more like natural choices for self-care. I wasn’t trying to overhaul my entire routine overnight, but these little tweaks felt pretty intuitive, and really added up to help me stick with the challenge, and feel more energized and clear-headed throughout the day.

Industry observers note that okay, so full transparency: I didn’t just wake up one day and bust out 21 straight three-milers. I eased in by starting off slow to establish a fresh routine, and listening to my body along the way. Here’s how to start running three miles a day—without burning out.

In a recent development, pro tip: “If you’re just starting out, alternate running days with walking or strength training to let your body adjust,” run coach Corky Corkum, CPT, previously told WH. “The number one reason fresh runners quit is injury or burnout from doing too much too soon.”.

Usually, it’s only a thin layer of ice on top or a clogged nozzle, but that’s enough to be annoying. If you ride at low enough temperatures with standard plastic bottles filled with plain water, it will inevitably happen. However, it’s notable to stay hydrated on winter rides.

It has been revealed that there are proven ways to keep your bottles from freezing—or carry hot beverages on rides. Hot chocolate, coffee, tea, or Skratch Labs’ apple cider will warm your soul and lift your mood. And nothing hits better than a coffee stop in the middle of a cold winter ride, especially when conditions are dreary or sloppy.

According to recent reports, stainless insulated bottles broke into cycling about five years ago and have since exploded in popularity. They’re a proven way to keep water and hydration mix cool on the hottest summer days, and they can also keep hot drinks warm for many miles on winter rides.

The Bivo Trio Bottle, available in raw stainless steel and silicone-covered stainless steel versions, has become a bottle of choice on cold-weather rides. Read on to find out why, plus tips to prevent your bottles from freezing this winter.

FULL COLD WEATHER BOTTLE TEST RESULTS.

Cyclists have many different methods (often handed down from one generation of riders to the next) to help prevent frozen bottles. One simple solution is to start your ride with hot water. However, depending on the temperature and ride length, this can also freeze.

Using insulated plastic bottles, adding a high-sodium drink mix, and wearing a hydration pack or vest under a riding jacket are all tricks I’ve used (with varying degrees of success) to keep my bottles from freezing. And some riders still swear by adding a shot of booze to their bidon. However, while these methods may prevent icing, they still result in a cold beverage during your ride.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to miss the growing popularity of stainless steel water bottles in cycling. Their use has boomed in the last few seasons as more riders have become concerned about microplastic contamination. Plus, these metal bidons, particularly the Bivo bottles, are in the cages of many cycling influencers.

Stainless bottles typically feature a vacuum-sealed double-wall design with a coated outer and a bare stainless inner layer. Since metal bottles are rigid, you cannot squeeze them like plastic bottles. (It takes some getting used to if you haven’t ridden them before.) And while stainless bottles are much heavier than plastic models, they are heavy-duty and almost indestructible—they dent and scratch but rarely break.

Bivo is the trend-setting stainless option and commonly available from retailers like REI, Backcountry, Amazon, or your local bike shop. The Insulated Mini we tested is 17 ounces and costs $44, or opt for the 21-ounce model for $5 more.

Sources indicate that I have ridden with insulated bottles at several points in my cycling life. But until last summer, I usually stuck with non-insulated plastic bottles for most of my rides, regardless of air temperature.

It has been revealed that generally, I prefer the feel of a regular bottle; 22-ounce Specialized Purist bottles are my go-to, and I occasionally carry a 10-ounce Purist Maker mug for a mid-ride coffee break. But I often skip stainless insulated bottles because they aren’t squeezable and weigh noticeably more than plastic bidons.

In a recent development, however, before a recent ride on a cold and blustery day, I filled an insulated bottle with hot chocolate and was pleased to have a warm treat throughout my 90-minute ride. So, like my insulated bottle test last summer, I applied a little science to see which insulated stainless bottles performed best in cold temps.

For this test, I gathered several popular metal insulated bottles. First, I evaluated the bottles by measuring water temperature over three hours in subfreezing conditions. Then, I used them on rides in cold weather to determine which worked best from a functional perspective.

While the intent was somewhat scientific, I also strove to be practical—these are tests anyone can do at home. This testing was not performed in a controlled environment or with professional-level, calibrated equipment.

Since it was below 32 degrees outside, I was able to perform outdoor freeze testing. Like my summer insulated bottle tests, I filled the selected bottles with 400 grams of tap water (heated to 212 degrees for this test instead of chilled water used in summer). Then I placed the filled bottles on my front porch in subfreezing temperatures; I did this after sunset so sunlight would not warm the bottles. Every 30 minutes, I checked and recorded the water temperature of each bottle, in the same order each time, with a digital food thermometer.

It has been revealed that following the initial three-hour test period, the bottles remained overnight in sub-freezing temperatures for an additional nine hours. This tested whether the contents would stay warm for a full 12 hours (as per some bottle makers’ claims). Additionally, for reference, I subjected a Purist Maker tumbler (with 200 grams of water), an insulated plastic bottle, and a standard plastic bottle to the same tests.

According to recent reports, the following day, I evaluated the bottles’ on-bike performance on a short loop in my neighborhood. I tested their use with standard and lobster-claw gloves (such as holding, opening caps, removing them from cages) and their nozzles’ function while drinking hot coffee (a medium-roast pour-over with some oat milk for my tests 😉).

Industry observers note that the results were clear: Insulated stainless bottles work very well in cold weather. They keep your beverage hot for an hour-long ride in 30-degree temps. For longer rides, your drink will experience some heat loss but will remain drinkably warm for three hours. The insulated metal bottles performed notably better than plastic bottles (insulated and non-insulated) for the full duration of the test.

Industry observers note that after about three hours of exposure in the cold, the Bivo Insulated Trio Mini kept my coffee at a warm 119.8 degrees. This is only slightly below coffee expert James Hoffmann’s recommended coffee-drinking temp of 122 to 129 degrees. (Although I’m not sure Hoffmann would be pleased drinking three-hour-old brew.) In 12-hour testing, none of the metal bottles froze. Most bottles finished at room temperature after 12 hours outside in freezing temperatures.

It has been revealed that on the bike, the Bivo valve works great, and the bottle texture isn’t overly slippery. The bottle shape is compatible with most cages, though it fits best in the Arundle Sport cage recommended by Bivo.

Sources indicate that nozzle Shield: Look for bottles with a cap that protects the nozzle. Typically, I’m not a fan of these shields when riding in warm weather—they flop around and get in the way when drinking. However, in the winter, caps keep road salt and slush off the bottle’s nozzle, and they also help prevent icing. Ones with a removable plastic or rubber shield are easier to clean; plus, you can use the bottles without the cap on warm days.

It has been revealed that vapor Pressure: Many of the tested bottles carry a warning about using liquids hotter than 180 degrees. This is to avoid scalding and burns from pressurized hot water when the cap or nozzle is opened. With insulated bottles, hot liquid heats the air inside the bottle enough to spray potentially near-boiling water into your mouth or onto your body.

Avoid this by letting your hot beverage cool slightly before pouring it into your bottle. For long rides (when using two bottles of hot drinks), save the hotter bottle for later in the day. This way, it has time to cool to a drinkable temperature.

It has been revealed that cage Compatibility: Since they do not deform or flex, metal bottles don’t pair with every bottle cage. Some stainless bottles have a loose fit in cages (bottles can even eject on rough roads), and some cage shapes do not allow some metal bottles to sit correctly, causing annoying rattling and buzzing while riding. Other cage-bottle pairings are so tight that it’s hard to remove the bottle while riding.

It has been revealed that my advice: Check that your cages work before dropping up to $100 for new bottles that won’t fit. Some brands have specific cage recommendations on their sites. You can also read user reviews for the compatibility of different bottles and cages. Also, be sure to check the overall bottle height to be sure it fits in your frame.

Recent findings suggest that dropped Bottles: I do not recommend using metal bottles in mass-start situations; use plastic bidons for massive group rides or races. When a metal bottle is ejected from a cage on a bump, or you drop one (as is prone to happen with cold hands or when wearing bulky gloves), it ricochets off the road surface more than a plastic bottle. And while metal makes these bottles more durable, they do not burst open on impact or crush if hit by other riders.

Bivo shook up the bottle market when it rolled out its stainless steel bottles. The small Richmond, Vermont-based company launched insulated bottles shortly after, and cyclists have fallen in love with them. They work well, look good, and don’t have a funky taste.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

  • Having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral.
  • "Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.
  • Sources indicate that the Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.

"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

Sources indicate that the Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and New York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.

Recent findings suggest that as far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.

In a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.

"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the Upcoming York Post.

Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.

In a recent development, she'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex.".

In a recent development, her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified.".

Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.

"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

Sager stated she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.

As for racing plans, Sager said she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:.

"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ.".

Industry observers note that sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#136997. Industry News: How Beginners Can Build Cycling Endurance in Just 3 Days a Week

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2022 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How Beginners Can Build Cycling Endurance in Just 3 Days a Week

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, building a base on the bike has traditionally meant putting in a lot of hours doing long, slow distance training.
  • Sources indicate that as it turns out, especially if you’re a newer cyclist, there’s a lot that you can accomplish if you only have three days a week to get on the bike.
  • Here, we spoke with Namrita Brooke, Ph.D., one of the lead coaches at BaseCamp, about how she would structure the optimal three-day week on the bike—and what other lifestyle tweaks she would make in order to improve fitness even when you can’t fit in long rides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, building a base on the bike has traditionally meant putting in a lot of hours doing long, slow distance training. But with work and family lives, it can feel impossible to find the hours in the week to properly commit to a base build, especially if you’re a beginner cyclist who’s not used to rides that take more than three hours.

Sources indicate that as it turns out, especially if you’re a newer cyclist, there’s a lot that you can accomplish if you only have three days a week to get on the bike. Building a base of fitness for cycling takes some commitment and consistency, but it doesn’t have to take over your life.

Here, we spoke with Namrita Brooke, Ph.D., one of the lead coaches at BaseCamp, about how she would structure the optimal three-day week on the bike—and what other lifestyle tweaks she would make in order to improve fitness even when you can’t fit in long rides.

In a recent development, A lot of cyclists think that if they can’t train 10-plus hours per week, their fitness will suffer, or they won’t make gains on the bike. This isn’t true, especially for newer riders. “Someone who has not been doing any exercise would see gains in as little as two to four hours a week of riding,” says Brooke. “If someone has some general fitness, gains could be had in four to six hours [per week].”.

Recent findings suggest that however, expect that after a few weeks or months, the tangible signs of progress will slow unless you can devote more time to training. “The tricky part is the ongoing gains might not be as easy to see as the initial gains,” Brooke adds. “Initially, if the athlete was measuring power, they would see power increases, but these would plateau in a few months, leading them to think gains are no longer occurring but in reality, the athlete is likely to still build other metrics of fitness like repeatability, durability, and resilience, but those are not as easy to measure.”.

According to recent reports, often, upcoming cyclists with limited time tend to attempt one monster ride on the weekend, skipping cycling during the week due to busy lives. But even if you can only eke out two one-hour (or 45-minute!) trainer sessions on weekdays in addition to the long weekend ride, you’ll gain fitness and strength faster than if you stick to a single ride.

“I would rather see the athlete do three quality days a week versus one or even two longer days,” says Brooke.

Industry observers note that “The base training goal, whether you’re a pro or average Joe, is to build the best aerobic fitness you can for the training hours you have available,” claims Brooke. Without this aerobic fitness, you won’t be able to boost your speed or power on the bike.

This means spending the bulk of your time on the bike in zone 2 (whether you use power, heart rate or perceived exertion). Riding in zone 2—also known as your endurance pace—will mean that you’re able to hold a conversation and speak in full sentences, but it should feel slightly difficult to do so. If you can chat away easily, you’re riding a little too easy. If you’re gasping for air between sentences, you’re riding a little too hard.

Recent findings suggest that by that, we mean your skin. Riding more miles means being aware of skin considerations such as sun protection and chafing prevention. Don’t just ignore reddened skin, use lubricants and padded shorts to feel more comfortable on the bike.

For newer riders, opt for the longer durations in each phase. If you’ve been riding for a while, you’ll likely notice that after a few weeks in each phase, you’re at a point where you’re not noticing any improvements—in that case, proceed to the next phase. Here’s how Brooke would break it down.

2.5-3.5 hours (zone 2), based on how much free time you have available.

Newly introduced riders may need to break up the zone 3 portion of the ride with an easy 5-10 minutes in the middle.

2.5-4 hour (zone 2) based on how much free time you have available.

Have an extra hour on Saturday for your long ride? Great! Woke up an hour early on Wednesday and have time to hop on the trainer for an extra 45-minute ride in zone 2? Fantastic. Feel free to add time whenever possible.

Four days on the bike is better than three, claims Brooke. “Two harder interval days and two longer days would be best if possible,” she notes. And this is actually a fairly standard schedule for most serious cyclists—they’ll add one or two additional easy rides to the schedule, but the meat and potatoes of their training consists of two longer endurance rides and two harder interval-based sessions.

Sources indicate that in fact, Brooke says that often, she hears fresh cyclists say they only have four hours per week to train, but once they get going, they start to “find” extra time. “You would be surprised how many newer riders think they are limited to four to six hours a week but once they really get into cycling, they make accommodations to squeeze in an extra hour or two per week,” she says. “I see riders all the time start to wake up earlier to squeeze in additional ride time before they start the rest of the day!”.

In a recent development, and thanks to the prevalence of indoor trainers, it’s easier than ever to sneak in an extra hour or two on the bike during a weekend or early in the morning, even if you have work or childcare demands on your time. But don’t neglect outdoor riding, especially if your base-building goal is to be able to keep up on the local group ride or jump into a race. While indoor training builds fitness, it doesn’t help improve your skills for riding outdoors, so make time for at least one outdoor ride per week if at all possible.

There is one final caveat: It’s easy to get excited about the prospect of adding a monster ride to your weekend whenever possible, but these long rides aren’t easy. Four hours on the bike will feel very, very different from two hours. If riding for five hours on Saturday means you can barely walk for two days after, or it impacts your training the next week, back off.

In a recent development, long rides shouldn’t leave you flattened for days afterwards. If they do, you’re doing too much, too soon. And Brooke notes that the longer you ride, the more important it is to properly fuel that long effort!

The fastest way to improve your fitness is—again—by consistently training. But training doesn’t mean all-bike-all-the-time! Brooke says there are quite a few simple additions you can do on those non-cycling days to see gains on the bike.

Sources indicate that → Walk: Often on conference calls for work, or accompanying your kiddos to soccer practice? Walk and talk, or do laps around the field while you cheer. “Walking is more of an aerobic builder than people think and can be a gentle form of aerobic activity to accompany bike time,” Brooke claims.

For the office worker, treadmill desks are becoming more popular, and if you do want to put in more bike time and you have a stationary trainer, you can do some easy spinning while answering emails or brainstorming for that substantial presentation.

According to recent reports, → Strength Train: “Strength training can be added in as little as 15 minutes a day, three days a week if we are willing to change the paradigm of going to the gym and lifting heavy things,” notes Brooke. “Integrating just this small amount of functional strength into a base training program like we do at BaseCamp yields long-term benefits to your training and health.”.

You can do shortstrength sessions at home with just a couple of weights, or even bodyweight alone to get started.

In a typical training proposal, cyclists have three weeks of training followed by a rest week where they do only a couple of shorter, easier rides. When you’re only able to ride three days a week, there’s no reason to take a rest week—you’re already getting plenty of recovery time in the four days you’re off the bike.

“The low training stimulus is likely not enough to elicit a high enough super-compensation response to make the loss of fitness during a rest week worth it,” claims Brooke. (That noted, if you’re a beginner rider and find that after three weeks, you are feeling fatigued, you can dial down the duration or intensity for that fourth week—but stick to three rides if possible.).

Sources indicate that once you’ve done your base training for several weeks with your rides spread out through the week (i.e Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday), you may want to try switching things up. If you do have the ability to try out fresh riding days, it’s worth experimenting with doing mini-training blocks, i.e riding three days in a row, some weeks. This subtle shift changes your training stimulus by forcing your body to contend with the need for speedier recovery between rides.

According to recent reports, newer riders may find that it’s harder to recover between rides in these chunks, says Brooke. “The challenge of block training is the athlete needs a certain amount of base fitness to be able to respond and adapt to this type of stimuli and in this scenario,” she explains. “But testing the block process is the only way to find out how they tolerate it.”.

If you try riding three days in a row and feel exhausted, go back to your regular schedule and test again after another few weeks of consistent training.

Industry observers note that while it’s tempting to stay in the base phase forever, this training phase should really only last around eight weeks. At this point, your aerobic fitness is maximized (for now) and it’s time to focus on the development of “power.”.

“After the base phase comes the build phase, where the athlete wants to increase their sustainable max power for a range of times,” notes Brooke. “For a newer cyclist without a specific goal, focus on holding a higher wattage for five minutes to 40 minutes. This phase should be maintained as long as the athlete continues to see improvement, then once response begins to fade, move on to the next phases.”.

In a recent development, once you’ve plateaued your power gains, the final phase, typically utilized when “peaking” for an event would be the “speed” phase, explains Brooke. “Here, the cyclist would focus on improving shorter efforts of under five minutes and building anaerobic capacity to focus on performing better in events or group rides.”.

After your main event, whether it’s a race or group ride or even just spending four to six weeks focusing on upping your sprint power, it’s time to take a short break and then circle back to base phase.

The good news is that once you’ve completed this cycle, you’ll be pleasantly surprised at how much stronger you’re feeling on the bike the second time you tackle base training. While training phases are cyclical, your fitness grows as you spend more and more time on the bike, so no training phase will feel exactly the same.

#136996. Procrastinating Your Winter Runs? Here’s What Will Actually Get You Out the Door, According to a Sports Psychologist

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1309 w)
📖 Baca

Procrastinating Your Winter Runs? Here’s What Will Actually Get You Out the Door, According to a Sports Psychologist

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run.
  • Recent findings suggest that while this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run. Then winter arrives, the temperatures drop, and suddenly it’s three straight months of daily prerun procrastination: I look for any excuse, task, or chore to delay heading out into the cold or stepping on the treadmill.

Recent findings suggest that while this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run. Except by then, I’m crunched for time, it’s pitch-black outside, and the whole process has drained enough of my mental energy that I’d rather push those miles to tomorrow.

Sources indicate that I know I’m not alone: Even professional marathoners fall into the “run-crastination” spiral. Previously, Des Linden and Kara Goucher discussed their own experiences on their podcast, Nobody Asked Us with Des & Kara. Still, I’d much rather find a way to avoid getting sucked in so I can get on with my run and my day, and enjoy both a little more as a result.

So, I asked a sports psychologist what actually works to get you out the door in the winter when anything sounds better than a run—plus when it’s actually a better idea to skip the miles.

Industry observers note that the first step to beating prerun procrastination? Determine the reason you’re doing it. “Procrastination is usually one of two things,” Justin Ross, Psy.D., a clinical sports psychologist and UESCA-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World. “One: It’s an avoidance strategy, because what you’re about to do is uncomfortable, unpleasant, hard, or challenging. But, it can also signal toward a different need that’s not being met.”.

In the winter months—especially for driven runners coming off a fall marathon season—that other need can be rest. “True athletic wisdom is knowing the difference between when procrastination is avoidance, and when it’s a sign that you need something other than a run that day,” Ross explains.

In a recent development, gaining that wisdom as an athlete takes time, practice, and some trial and error. The best way to start? Focus on creating “systems” that make procrastination less likely so you can more easily identify the action that aligns with your needs, goals, and values, Ross notes. Most times, these systems (which we outline below) lead to better outcomes than trying to rely on willpower alone or following an impulse in the moment.

Sources indicate that if you find yourself avoiding a run, remove as many obstacles as possible that stand between you and getting out the door or to the gym. For Ross, that means setting out all his running clothes and fuel ahead of time so he doesn’t need to hunt for that one pair of gloves he hasn’t seen since last January.

“Without preparation, procrastination becomes a whole lot easier because you have all these extra hurdles,” he explains. “When it’s dark and cold in the winter, you need to problem-solve in ways that you don’t need to when it’s beautiful out and you’re excited to run.”.

For me, that means making sure my headlamp actually has working batteries if I’m planning to run outside in the evenings. If I’m hitting the treadmill, I cue up a playlist, TV show, or podcast on my phone and stock my gym bag with a postrun snack and a full water bottle.

When you’re procrastinating a run, try shifting your focus from what you’re doing to why you’re doing it. “Remind yourself why this run is notable to you or how it helps you,” Ross says. For example, you might think about your values or current goals and consider how this workout brings you closer to them.

I’ve found I’m motivated simply by the fact that running makes me feel like my favorite version of myself—and that boosts my mood more than any race-specific or fitness goal. But you might be more excited by the idea that staying consistent with your training over the winter will set you up for a stronger chance at a marathon PR in the spring.

Industry observers note that consider what might add a little bit more spark to your routine or make it more enticing. You might decide to meet up with a friend or local run club for a few miles. You might look forward to your treadmill run as “the 30 minutes of my day where I don’t have to be bothered and I can just watch my favorite show [alone],” notes Ross.

The reward mindset helps you refocus on what brings you joy, instead of just relieving the pressure of needing to get in a workout.

Another helpful strategy? Doing the absolute bare minimum. “Runners often fall into this trap of having rigid rules around their exercise or their training,” says Ross. Try letting go of whatever mileage or workout you had planned for the day, and tell yourself that you’ll just run for 10 minutes and then reassess how you feel.

Industry observers note that you may even want to adjust your whole training standard ahead of the winter season, Ross says. For example, you might reduce the length, intensity, or frequency of the workouts you initiative to do each week. Or, instead of targeting a specific pace or mileage requirement, run or cross-train solely based on time. “Think about being more flexible in your approach during the winter months. Maybe you aim for the minimal effective dose to get the benefit you’re looking for, like just running for 20 minutes if your usual standard is 60,” Ross suggests.

Ross explains that winter can be a meaningful time for runners to examine what rules they have around their training that might be adding pressure. For example, I used to follow a silly rule from an old college teammate who said that any run shorter than three miles “didn’t count” as a true run. Once I finally let go of that, I found it much easier to get moving—even if it was just for an easy walk in the park near my house.

“This time of year, see how you can approach exercise from an overall health or mood-boost perspective instead of a training perspective,” suggests Ross.

Also, question any rigid rules you’ve established for yourself around volume, pace, or mileage—like making sure to hit a specific number of miles every week or setting a minimum pace requirement for all your runs—because they may backfire and lead to mental burnout over the long term, he claims.

Sources indicate that if you’ve done all the above and you still can’t get yourself out the door, a run may not actually be what you need. “If you keep hitting the moment to head out and that intuitive voice notes, ‘I just really don’t want to,’ try listening to that voice. Listen to your body,” Ross suggests. “It’s okay to give yourself permission for rest and recovery—especially during this time of year.”.

Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that glute bridge post-run.
  • Industry observers note that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a upcoming study on anti-movement vs.
  • It has been revealed that “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

Industry observers note that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a upcoming study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

It has been revealed that “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

Recent findings suggest that when we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

Why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly notable for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

When running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

According to recent reports, while running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

While some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

Enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an important role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

In a recent development, runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

Best Winter Cycling Gloves for Cold, Wet, and Windy Rides

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers.
  • Industry observers note that the right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers. Besides being uncomfortable, numb hands can make it difficult to shift gears or feel your brake levers, turning a cold ride into a potentially unsafe one.

Industry observers note that the right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls. But finding that pair isn’t always as simple as checking the temperature rating on the packaging. How warm your hands get, the weather conditions, and the type of riding you do all play a role.

For example, on a 35-degree road ride, you’ll likely want a much warmer glove than you would for a mountain bike ride at the same temperature. Higher speeds on the road mean more windchill, while a slower, harder effort on the trails can leave your hands sweaty in gloves that are too warm. If you ride throughout the winter, it’s worth owning a few different pairs to cover the range of conditions you’ll encounter.

Sources indicate that I tested more than 40 glove models in temperatures ranging from the low 60s to below 20 degrees, then narrowed the field to my six favorites. I’ve included recommended temperature ranges for each, but consider those a starting point. If you tend to run cold or have Raynaud’s syndrome, you may want a warmer glove; if your hands sweat easily, a lighter, more breathable option might work better.

Sources indicate that more Winter Gear Advice: Our Expert Swears by This Three-Layer Trick. ● The Best Men’s Winter Cycling Jackets ● The Best Winter Cycling Hats.

Perhaps my all-time favorite version of my all-time favorite glove, DeFeet’s Duraglove has been around for ages and has remained mostly unchanged. It’s very comfortable, has great dexterity, and provides good grip. Plus, it has touchscreen functionality. DeFeet offers two versions of this glove: The plain Duraglove ET and the Duraglove ET Wool Blend featured here, which uses a merino wool blend.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve found this version to be the warmer of the two. I’ve worn this glove into the low 40s during high-intensity rides and stayed comfortable. Because this knit glove is incredibly breathable, it’s still comfortable to wear as the day warms into the mid-to-high 50s. The Duraglove is unsuitable for rainy rides as its knit construction will quickly soak up water.

According to recent reports, these Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be as warm as they are. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no issues.

They use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a major fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

Near-freezing temperatures with rain are probably the most challenging conditions to ride in. But for some, it’s unavoidable. Glacier Glove’s Ice Bay is as good as it gets for these conditions. It’s constructed with 2mm-thick, fleece-lined neoprene and is as waterproof as any piece of clothing could be.

In a recent development, these gloves have incredible dexterity given their warmth. The long cuff is easy to tuck under your rain jacket to keep water out. The downside of a neoprene glove is that it does not breathe at all. That’s partly how it keeps your hands warm, but it only works as long as you keep the gloves on. If you take them off, your now-sweaty hands will get quite cold quickly, and your formerly toasty gloves (lacking body heat) will be cold and wet with sweat. Despite these drawbacks, if it’s cold and rainy and I need to be out riding, these are the gloves I reach for.

In a recent development, these pricey gloves are the warmest five-finger gloves I’ve tried that still let me move my fingers. Gore took inspiration from high alpine mountaineering for the design. The outer shell uses a Gore-Tex ePE liner that is highly wind- and water-resistant. For insulation, Gore used a PrimaLoft lining. It features one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios. All of this results in a glove that can be comfortable down to and below freezing, depending on your pace and specific riding conditions.

According to recent reports, I’ve used similarly warm gloves from other brands, and they've often been far too bulky to feel useful. These still maintain a good bar feel and let me freely articulate my fingers. While they have touchscreen compatibility, I found them a little too bulky to promptly type out a text message on an iPhone.

According to recent reports, we’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

In a recent development, the gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

In a recent development, the secret to the dexterity is the PrimaLoft Gold insulation, which provides exceptional warmth without adding bulk. Most very warm gloves are also very thick, which makes it difficult to locate the proper shifter and grip your brake levers. This pair keeps my hands warm on long weekend rides and daily commutes, even when temperatures dip below freezing, without getting in the way.

Recent findings suggest that bar Mitts may look unconventional, but riders who use them swear by their added warmth and control. Designed to work with gloves, these neoprene covers attach to your bar and enclose your bike’s shifters and brake levers. They add significant wind protection and help keep your hands shielded from the elements.

Industry observers note that several Bar Mitt variants are available for road, mountain, and townie-style handlebars. Be sure to check details and confirm fitment with your bar/shifter combo before you order.

Glove fit is subjective. They should fit in the Goldilocks range. If your gloves are too significant, you risk losing grip on the handlebar and controls. But a glove that’s too tight can prevent you from comfortably grasping the handlebar or grips.

According to recent reports, an easy way to spot a glove that’s too major is if you have a lot of fabric bunching in your palm. It’s always worth trying new gloves on your bike to see how they feel on the bars, since labeled sizing can differ from brand to brand.

If you’re riding in temperatures below the mid-40s or closer to freezing, you want a glove with some insulation. In the most basic definition, insulation is filling used to capture and hold onto warmth. The most familiar insulation for outdoor use is down, often found in puffy jackets. In gloves, you are most likely to find down in very bulky mittens, which are very warm but lack the dexterity for cycling.

According to recent reports, most cycling-specific gloves use synthetic insulation from companies like Polartech or PrimaLoft. These materials are most often used on the back of the hand to protect from wind and minimize interference with the handlebar feel. Thin, grippy material is generally found on the palm. Many brands use leather on the palms for improved grip and durability, so watch out for this if you avoid buying animal products.

For the interior of the glove, look for polyester or Merino wool. You want something that wicks sweat and keeps your hands dry—sweaty hands can promptly turn into frozen prunes.

Recent findings suggest that gloves with appropriate breathability for the temperature and your riding effort keep your hands warm and dry. The warmer the temps, or the higher your effort, the more breathable you’ll want your gloves.

Regionally, humidity also plays a part in selecting the right glove. If you ride somewhere cool and dry, such as Colorado, where it might be in the 30s with low humidity, you likely will be able to use a lighter pair of more breathable gloves. These can do a much better job keeping you warm because they transfer moisture away from your hands more effectively. If you ride in the Northeast, the same pair of gloves might feel too cold at the same temperature, since humidity is often much higher. For these conditions, you’ll want a glove with better wind and waterproofing at the expense of breathability.

Once you figure out the glove warmth you need for your riding, consider other features before buying. Something I find very important in gloves meant for frigid weather is long cuffs. Cuffs make it easy to tuck the glove under or sometimes over your jacket sleeve, keeping your wrists warm and stopping cold air from entering your jacket.

Industry observers note that the palm construction of a glove is also worth careful examination. A common feature is padding. Some riders prefer padded gloves, while others do not. Padding matters less the warmer a glove gets, since the palm becomes bulkier with insulation. For thinner gloves, a seamless palm is the way to go. It minimizes any chance of irritation and improves handlebar feel.

If you ride with a smartphone or have a touchscreen computer, gloves that interact with these devices are great. The less you need to remove your gloves in the cold, the happier your hands will be.

Finally, a soft, large terrycloth nose-wipe section (preferably along the thumb or index finger) is good if you’re a heavy snotter.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Fresh York City bike messenger but promptly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.
