  • Industry observers note that getting faster isn’t just about training harder.
  • While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that getting faster isn’t just about training harder. It also requires smarter recovery.

While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.

Major picture, recovery runs should help you stay consistent between harder sessions; they shouldn’t leave you carrying extra fatigue into your next workout. However, simply running at an easy pace doesn’t guarantee an easy training load because the longer you run, the more energy you use and the more repetitive impact you take on.

Industry observers note that so how long should your recovery runs last to maintain the volume-building, bloodflow-boosting benefits? And what signs mean it’s time to cut the run short?

We asked run coaches and exercise physiologists to explain how to find the right recovery run duration to ensure you’re not dragging for your next workout and when calling it a (rest) day might work best.

Recovery runs allow runners to increase their overall aerobic training volume without taking a complete rest day after every hard session, claims run coach, author, and founder of 80/20 Endurance, Matt Fitzgerald. For instance, if the sole objective were to recover from quality runs as quickly as possible, total rest (a.k.a. not running at all) is more effective.

But receiving the benefits of recovery runs without elevating fatigue or injury risk depends on keeping duration within a certain range.

It has been revealed that “As a run extends, we’re also continuing to consume energy and introduce mechanical load,” explains Pamela Geisel, CSCS, RRCA-certified run coach, exercise physiologist, and director of Performance and Wellness Services at the Hospital for Special Surgery in Newly introduced York City. In other words, your muscles are still contracting, your body is still using fuel, and your bones, tendons, and joints are absorbing the repetitive impact of every stride.

If you extend a recovery run too long, the stress caused by this additional workload begins to outweigh the aerobic benefits of the run and can lead to the aforementioned heightened fatigue and injury risk, especially if you’re recovering from a particularly demanding training session.

According to recent reports, this logic is exactly why experts all agree that recovery runs absolutely can go on for too long. The tricky part is finding the line.

“There’s no established duration or mileage at which an easy run becomes detrimental to recovery,” states Michael Landram, an exercise physiologist and assistant professor at the University of Scranton.

Instead, each person’s ideal duration depends on a variety of factors, including training history, current fatigue, nutrition, sleep, and the demands of any upcoming workouts, Landram explains.

Here’s a three-step checklist for making sure yours fall in the right range.

Usually, Geisel recommends keeping recovery runs between 20 and 40 minutes in length, but that window should shift depending on how much you’re accustomed to running.

For example, if you’re averaging around 20 miles per week, Geisel suggests aiming for approximately 15 to 25 minutes. If you’re regularly logging up to 60 miles per week, you can pencil in 25- to 45-minute recovery sessions.

And remember, these recommendations are starting points, not strict limits. Danny Mackey, head coach of the Brooks Beasts Track Club, notes he might prescribe a recovery run of just 20 minutes for an 800-meter specialist, while long-distance runners accustomed to running 75 to 80 miles per week can comfortably handle a 60-minute recovery run.

Additionally, it’s vital to take into consideration how long you’ve maintained your current weekly mileage.

Landram explains that a runner who’s consistently logged 50-mile weeks for several years may tolerate longer recovery runs than someone who’s only recently built up to that level. Even if both runners in this example have similar cardiovascular fitness, their muscles may not be equally adapted to the repetitive demands of 50-mile weeks.

So, if you’ve recently increased your weekly mileage, stick to shorter recovery runs and gradually extend their duration as your body adjusts.

Industry observers note that if you’re relatively fresh to running, are only running a few days per week, or have only easy runs on your schedule as you build endurance and consistency, you may not need a dedicated recovery run at all. Rest days allow for proper rejuvenation between workouts.

Fitzgerald recommends using your typical easy-run duration as a reference point and making recovery runs shorter and slower (zone 1, anyone?). If your scheduled easy runs are usually 60 minutes long, for instance, a recovery run—particularly one scheduled after hard, quality workouts—might last 40 minutes or less, at an even lower intensity.

It has been revealed that if you’ve just completed a particularly demanding interval session, long run, or race, consider keeping your recovery run at the shorter end of your usual range. The same applies if you have another hard workout scheduled within the next 24 to 48 hours.

Heat, hills, and uneven terrain can also make an otherwise easy session more taxing, so it’s worth considering an even shorter duration in those circumstances.

Overall, your recovery-run duration should reflect what your body is accustomed to handling, rather than a mileage target you’re trying to reach.

Even if you’ve planned your recovery run carefully, it’s notable to pay attention to how your body responds once you start moving.

Sources indicate that one of the first warning signs is a change in perceived exertion. If your usual recovery pace suddenly feels harder than it should or your legs feel unusually heavy, you may need to reconsider how long you’re running.

Geisel also recommends paying attention to changes in your stride, including heavier foot strikes and other form problems getting worse as the run progresses.

The metrics available on your watch can also indicate a recovery run has gone too long. For example, an unusually elevated heart rate at your normal easy pace may signal you’re carrying too much fatigue, Landram explains. Though remember heat, dehydration, sleep, and stress can also affect heart rate, so pair it with how you feel to determine if you’re going too long.

According to recent reports, if you’re feeling unusually tired during a recovery run, Shannon Hugard, a biomechanics researcher at the University of Oregon, recommends a simple midrun check-in. “If you’re feeling more fatigued or sore than usual, run that first mile,” she advises. “See how you’re feeling. If you’re still sore or fatigued, cut that easy run duration by about 25 to 50 percent.” If you’re experiencing pain that affects your stride, however, it’s better to stop immediately rather than push through.

It’s also worth paying attention to how you feel after your recovery run.

In a recent development, for Mackey, the biggest giveaway that an athlete isn’t recovering adequately is often what happens during their next hard workout. “If they’re struggling to hit their usual paces, feeling unusually fatigued, or showing a noticeable drop in motivation, I know it’s time to reassess their recovery sessions,” he indicates.

It has been revealed that if these warning signs persist, the best option might just be skipping your next recovery run altogether. A rest day, walk, or low-impact cross-training session can give your body a break from the repetitive loading of running, particularly when you’re dealing with lingering fatigue.

And if you think cutting a run short feels like a missed training opportunity, take a cue from the pros: “This is one of the biggest differences I see in elite runners,” indicates Fitzgerald. “They take pride in their restraint and ability to hold back, because they know it’s part of a more intentional proposal.”.

Research Reveals This Is the Best Way to Balance Strength Training and Running

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time.
  • But sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles.
  • Industry observers note that so if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time. Combining strength training and a running schedule means you boost your fitness in multiple ways.

But sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles. This isn’t just in your head. According to a review of 132 studies, it takes a full day or two more to recover from resistance training than it does a high-intensity run.

Industry observers note that so if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training. Not only does it just feel good to move your muscles through full ranges of motion, especially after sitting all day, but it can also pay off in the long run for your run performance and overall health. In fact, several studies point to better running economy, as well as VO2 max and anaerobic threshold, when following a program that incorporates both endurance training and strength training.

Instead of ditching strength exercises to focus on mileage, the key is creating a strength training schedule that optimally fits into your run training. After all, strength training is supposed to help, not harm, your running. Here’s how to achieve that.

It has been revealed that get the strength initiative that works for all runners! Race-Ready Strength, our newly introduced progressive 4-week training program, will get you in the best shape to reach your racing goals.

To get it right, you need to understand how your body reacts to moving heavy stuff. Picture pushing a hand truck 50 feet. Pretty easy. That’s running—your body is the hand truck and it moves its own weight rather effortlessly. Now slide the hand truck under a fridge and push it just five feet. A lot more difficult. That’s mechanical loading; it’s why 10 heavy squats feels so much more challenging than 1,000 foot strikes.

The reason strength training makes you faster is because it lowers the amount of energy required to hit a certain pace, explains Kenji Doma, Ph.D., a sports and exercise scientist at James Cook University in Queensland, Australia, and author of a 2014 study on strength training and running performance published in the European Journal of Sports Science.

It has been revealed that doma has also studied the effects of combining aerobic exercise and strength training on muscle hypertrophy and strength, as published in a Sports Medicine systematic review and meta-analysis in 2022. The researchers found that combining the two types of training doesn’t hinder strength and muscle-building gains, but can compromise explosive strength gains when performed in the same session—something to consider if that’s your goal.

What’s important to note is that when you lift weights, your brain alters its neural recruitment pattern, calling up the most fatigue-resistant muscle fibers so you exert less energy. That’s why you don’t want to skimp on strength training. Doma’s research offers guidance on how best to combine mile repeats and repetitions in the gym for a more well-rounded running and strength training schedule.

Industry observers note that in the study that focused specifically on running performance, 15 runners of a wide range of ability and average weekly mileage did different strength-training sessions on three occasions. One workout was a high-intensity, total-body session, one was high intensity but for legs only, and one was a low-intensity, total-body workout.

Six hours after each workout, the runners did a treadmill test for 10 minutes at 70 percent of ventilatory threshold pace (easy), then 10 minutes at 90 percent of threshold pace (roughly close to half marathon pace), and then as long as possible at 110 percent of threshold pace. The runners also did the treadmill test at the outset of the study, to get a benchmark for how they would perform when fresh.

Sources indicate that the high-intensity strength workouts significantly lessened the runners’ time to exhaustion at the end of the treadmill test. In the benchmark test, they’d lasted an average of close to five minutes at 110 percent of threshold pace. After each of the high-intensity strength sessions, time to exhaustion was almost a minute less, suggesting that the hard weight workouts six hours earlier had dramatically decreased the runners’ ability to sustain fast running.

Doma says his findings have practical implications for how runners should arrange their workouts.

Recent findings suggest that first, he advises not to schedule a hard running workout later in the day of a weight session. “Running at maximal effort is impaired six hours [after] lower-extremity resistance training, and therefore trained to moderately-trained runners will need more than that to recover for running sessions set at high intensities,” he says.

Plus, running at maximal effort is still impaired 24 hours after lower-extremity resistance training, according to Doma. “Therefore, in the case of trained and moderately-trained runners undertaking high-intensity running sessions after lower-extremity resistance training, they may need more than one day to recover.”.

Doma also found that running performance at lower intensities was unaffected by the weight workouts. “Runners could undertake strength training and running sessions on the same day six hours apart as long as the running session is set at submaximal intensities,” Doma indicates. In other words, if you have an easy, long run, or recovery run on the schedule, it’ll be fine to double up that day, as long as workouts are more than six hours apart.

If possible, Doma suggests arranging your schedule so that on days that you run and lift, running comes first. “I found that lower-extremity resistance training performed six hours prior to running sessions at moderate to high intensities cause carryover effects of fatigue the next day to a greater extent than the reverse sequence,” he says. “Therefore, if undertaking lower-extremity resistance training and running sessions on the same day, it is best to undertake a running session before a strength training session. For example, running in the morning before work and lower-extremity resistance training in the evening after work.”.

In this scenario, it would make sense to have that morning run be one of your harder workouts of the week. Your workout the following day would then be an easy recovery run, which would be warranted even without the evening lifting, but is that much more called for on the basis of Doma’s research.

This sequence would also mesh with many coaches’ recommendation to have great discrepancy between your hard and easy days, so that you can better recover from your toughest workouts—instead of including hard elements of non-running training on your easy running days.

It has been revealed that scott is a veteran running, fitness, and health journalist who has held senior editorial positions at Runner’s World and Running Times. Much of his writing translates sport science research and elite best practices into practical guidance for everyday athletes. He is the author or coauthor of several running books, including Running Is My Therapy, Advanced Marathoning, and Meb for Mortals. Scott has also written about running for Slate, The Atlantic, the Washington Post, and other members of the sedentary media. His lifetime running odometer is past 110,000 miles, but he’s as much in love as ever.

Reviewed: The EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone.
  • In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.
  • Before we dive into the science, an vital clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone. At the opposite end of the spectrum, swimming in very warm water can also crater your comfort and results. That’s why we were psyched to test the EZ Hydro-Glide Cap, a one-of-a-kind attempt to boost swimming performance and safety using wearable technology designed to enhance thermoregulation.

In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.

Before we dive into the science, an vital clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap. More on that below.

It has been revealed that but first, kudos to EZ Gains, a popular outside-the-box triathlon retailer, for attacking a problem that numerous triathletes experience – significant discomfort when swimming in very cold and very warm water. We’ve learned a lot in recent years about thermoregulation, and any improvements in this area could help many athletes, including friends of mine who’ve quit the sport after repeated unpleasant swims.

Industry observers note that EZ Gains’ approach is based on credible science. The manufacturer notes that your head plays an outsized role in your body’s response to ambient temperatures, given the extensive network of blood vessels and nerves just beneath your scalp. This rings true, as does the contention that regulating the temperature difference between the water and your head – both the initial gap and the ongoing variance – can mitigate the downsides of extreme heat and cold.

In a recent development, we use insulated neoprene caps for chilly swims, after all. What if a single, more sophisticated solution helped us thrive in both polar and equatorial waters?

EZ Gains’ answer is a honeycombed high-tech foam and hard plastic wedge that sits at the top of your forehead under an (included) standard swim cap. Before putting it on, you can place one or two small thermal packs (also included) inside the hollow center of the wedge. These packs – and an additional thin heating strip – provide a cooling or warming effect as needed. In warm water, you can use a frozen pack or two to cool your forehead, which is meant to keep your core temp down and reduce heat fatigue.

You’re also supposed to use frozen packs when swimming in frigid water – say 60 degrees F or less – according to EZ Gains. The idea is to pre-condition your head to the chilly temps you’re about to encounter. This may sound counterintuitive, but EZ Gains notes the pre-cooling technique can prevent cold shock, a serious autonomic response that elevates your heart rate and can cause panic and even cardiac arrest. The packs can also be heated for a touch of warmth when facing cool-but-not-arctic conditions.

For more preparation for swimming in cold water, read: How to Acclimate and Prepare for Cold-Water Triathlons.

To evaluate the system, I tested it in various bodies of water over the course of five months, from midsummer to late autumn. My primary locations were indoor and outdoor pools in Boulder, Colorado, and our local reservoir. Water temperatures ranged from 84 degrees F all the way down to 50 degrees F. All of my swims were 45-90 minutes long, more than enough to mimic race conditions and assess how well the device limits heat and cold stress.

Industry observers note that the TLDR from my testing: Some upcoming technologies sound great on paper but don’t pan out in real life. Sadly, this device is one of those. On two of its three core value propositions, the Hydro-Glide fell short. I’ll tackle them one by one.

Recent findings suggest that first, EZ Gains indicates the cap will reduce heat fatigue and related complications – anxiety, increased heart rate, dehydration, and confusion – when using the frozen packs. I did notice a cooling sensation in the early parts of my summer swims, typically lasting 10-15 minutes. But while I appreciated the initial cooling, I didn’t discern a material difference in fatigue, judgment, or heart rate after an hour, even during my most intense workouts.

It has been revealed that second, the cap is supposed to prevent the instant discomfort and cold shock that many people experience when diving into frigid water. Perhaps I’m less sensitive than other athletes (my long-suffering wife might have an opinion on this), but using slightly thawed ice packs to pre-cool my head (as instructed) didn’t eliminate the ice cream headaches.

In my experience, this kind of pain starts in my face and forehead, neither of which are protected by the device. It’s possible that the Hydro-Glide would help other swimmers, since physiological reactions vary widely, but I’d speculate that too much of your face, forehead, and neck remain exposed for the cold to be significantly neutralized.

Third, EZ Gains says the cap will protect your head when another swimmer clobbers you, which seems legit in the case of head-on impacts. A friend in my Masters group sustained a concussion last year when another swimmer swerved into her during a backstroke set. While I didn’t do any head-banging to test this claim, it’s reasonable to believe the Hydro-Glide’s foam would’ve absorbed that blow. Since the wedge doesn’t cover the sides or back of your head, though, it wouldn’t deflect all-too-common errant elbows or kicks to those areas during a race start.

There are two additional downsides to consider. If you have an XL melon like mine, you may experience discomfort from the pressure of the cone against your head. I did, typically after about 30 minutes. And if you’re even the slightest bit fashion-conscious, you will probably draw the line at looking like a Corythosaurus from Jurassic Park. The first time I showed up at the pool wearing the Hydro-Glide, several of my masters teammates burst out laughing. Someone compared me to a Conehead.

Which I could possibly live with if the results had been stellar. However, the Hydro-Glide didn’t deliver a meaningful upside for me versus a standard swim cap. While EZ Gains deserves praise for its waaay-out-of-the-box effort to improve swim safety and comfort, this product’s current execution doesn’t justify a $270 investment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that just as the seasons change, so do riders’ preferences of which types of riding are preferred. For some, the season for taking the road bike on the local roads starts to fade as temperatures get colder and the gravel trail that parallels the road gets more appealing every degree cooler. It’s time to turn the road bike onto that gravel path.

Many of us have tried to take our road bikes on gravel, and there are steps you can take to get the most out of that underbiked gravel ride. After a recent lunch ride, the question was asked, “how much gravel can you take a road bike on?” Since gravel means different things to different people the easy answer is, it depends, but I wanted to stress test my road bike to find out.

I remember an old-school bike technician I used to work with told me, “you can ride any bike on anything if you are light on the bike and find the right line.” While that may be true, I wanted to find out how I could most comfortably take my road bike on everything that is off-road.

Industry observers note that after taking my road bike where it was not designed to go, I learned some limitations as well as some simple part swaps to get the most versatility out of a road bike. Below I’ll touch on those limitations that I found and give you the most impactful changes you can make to your road bike before taking it on gravel. As Doc says to Marty McFly in Back to the Future, “Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.”.

The bike I decided to do the testing on is my Trek Madone, and I’ve had 700x28mm Pirelli P Zero Race tires pretty much since I’ve built up the bike. Those are by far my favorite road tires for all-around road riding—they’re fast, grip well through turns, and are surprisingly durable for performing so well.

In a recent development, even though I love those Pirellis for road riding most of the year, I knew I would want to have extra rubber when I’m chattering along through some of the chunkier gravel I’d be testing on. I decided to swap out my tires for a set of the Continental Grand Prix 5000 in 700x32 mm. The maximum tire width on the Gen 8 Trek Madone is 32mm, but these Continental tires only measure just over 30mm because of the internal rim width on the stock Bontrager wheels. I could probably bump up the width a bit more, but I decided to keep the 32mm just in case I knock the wheels out of true during the stress testing.

Going wider with your tires adds an extra bit of compliance and more contact patch—both will help your ride quality when you take your road bike out on gravel. Part of the trick with going wider and bumping down your tire pressure is to make sure your tires are set up as tubeless. Setting your tires up tubeless allows you to run a lower tire pressure without the risk of pinch flats.

When you take your road bike on gravel, upcoming bar tape can help by decreasing a little bit of the vibration. As you ride, most bar tapes compress a bit from the constant pressure of your hands. Some tapes may even start to unravel in sections where you keep your hands a lot—we used to see this a lot when customers couldn’t comfortably reach the hoods. There would be visible wear marks where the rider was keeping their hands on the bars. So replacing your tape at least once a season is a good idea to keep comfort up.

Out of all the bar tape that I’ve tried my favorite for taking a road bike on gravel is the Lizard Skin 3.2 mm Bar Tape. The slightly thicker tape reduces a bit of the chatter in your hands and it’s tacky enough that your hands stay stuck to the bars when you need them to be. This is true on wider tire gravel bikes as well, but it’s especially noticeable when you don’t have the same vibration dampening from a wider tire.

Flat tires happen on any bike, but they can be even more common rolling down a chunky gravel road on your road bike. Correct tire choice, tubeless setups, and riding a bit more cautiously than normal will all help prevent a ride-ending flat tire.

Industry observers note that if you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multitool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

If you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multi tool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

According to recent reports, keep in mind it’s still possible to get flat tires with tubeless tires. A few years ago I took my road bike out on a local gravel ride and I bumped my tire pressure down to have a little more comfort and traction on my skinny road tires. I was rolling through some gravel and I hit a rock with my rear wheel hard enough for the tire to get pinched against the rim and put a good slice in my tire. Luckily I brought a tire boot (I used a dollar bill) and an extra tube so I was able to pedal back to the shop. In a pinch I’ve used things like candy wrappers or leaves as a very temporary tire boot. They don’t take up much room in your pack, so if you bring one in your pack there is no need to MacGyver anything on the side of the trail.

It has been revealed that if you only have a road bike and want to occasionally ride gravel I would strongly consider getting a second wheelset to ride gravel. If you have one wheel set for gravel and one for pavement you can easily swap wheel sets when you want to ride one discipline versus the other. Set up the wheels with a cassette with the same gear range, same size rotors, and the widest tires your frame and fork can fit—suddenly you have two bikes in one.

As I was taking my road bike on exceedingly questionable terrain I thought, what would most people actually be okay with riding this bike on? As I rolled my Madone into some singletrack it was swiftly apparent most people wouldn’t be stoked to follow behind me. Insufficient tire clearance, room for tread, and lack of suspension might be the first reasons you’d think of why a road bike isn’t going to perform well on singletrack (and you’re absolutely right). The geometry of the Madone didn’t give the handling needed to reasonably navigate through the tight trails in the woods.

The next category is where we start to delve into true gravel: doubletrack, jeep roads, and limited maintenance gravel. This is where I started to see the road bike actually perform reasonably well. The extra tire width combined with bumping down the tire pressure allowed the bike to feel reasonably compliant rolling through the varying surfaces. However, I really felt the times I caught a small rock that was hiding underneath the leaves.

Recent findings suggest that riding local gravel roads and canal trails may have been bumpy, but it was most certainly doable. I noticed I was bumping around a lot, and I felt like I was putting in more effort to match my typical effort on the same segments I usually ride with a gravel bike. Especially when I started to ride through gravel after a bit of rain or sections that were covered in wet leaves I wished for a wider tire with more tread. I had to keep some of the descents a little more tame compared to normal, but on my local gravel climbs I was rolling up faster and more efficiently than normal. That is, until my rear tire would lose traction and I would burn all my matches trying to keep the bike both upright and going up.

Even with that being the case, so many modern road bikes now offer tire clearance to get a cyclocross tire set up. If I were committing to my road bike as a gravel-to-road crossover bike for the winter I would set it up with some fast-rolling tubeless cyclocross tires, put on latest bar tape, put an extra tube in my flat pack, and let it ride.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

What Nike Shoe Matches Your Running Style?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, runners are a varied breed.
  • Luckily, there’s a Nike shoe to support your training goals, whether you run for fun or race competitively.
  • Recent findings suggest that you can depend on your daily run—it’s what gives you energy and lifts your mood, no matter what else the day may bring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, runners are a varied breed. Some crave the routine of a daily run and the endorphin boost it brings. Others may be training for an endurance event like a marathon or half marathon, with specific distance goals. You may be chasing a new PR, looking to hit the trails, or mixing running with other activities like lifting weights. So many different ways to run, so many shoes to choose from.

Luckily, there’s a Nike shoe to support your training goals, whether you run for fun or race competitively. Not sure which style fits your needs best? We’ve got you covered with the shopping guide below.

Recent findings suggest that you can depend on your daily run—it’s what gives you energy and lifts your mood, no matter what else the day may bring. The Nike Pegasus line has offered that same dependability for more than four decades, and the technology just keeps getting better.

Sources indicate that the reason why the Pegasus Plus 2 works for daily, all-purpose running is its technology: Superlight ZoomX foam in the heel pairs with an exposed Air Zoom unit in the forefoot to deliver comfort and energy return that powers up every mile. Up top, a sleek mesh material offers both support and flexibility without letting your foot overheat, while a revamped forefoot shape gives your toes a little more wiggle room. And the classic Waffle outsole design has an updated diagonal pattern with flex grooves for better traction and ground feel, so you’re more in tune with your terrain. Plus, those textured laces are less likely to come untied—so you’ve got one less thing to worry about when you’re heading out the door.

The Pegasus Plus 2 is also a good option to slip on for easy and slower recovery runs. Responsive and comfy without being super stacked, this shoe is the ultimate workhorse in your running closet.

According to recent reports, for long runs and marathon training, you want max cushioning, like what’s found in Nike’s Vomero 18. Lightweight ZoomX foam stacked on top of responsive ReactX foam in the shoe’s midsole results in a plushy landing that has you feeling like you’re landing on a cloud with every step. Considering that the Vomero 18 is 13 percent more responsive than previous React technology (per the company’s own measurement), your legs feel less fatigued even as the miles add up.

It has been revealed that an increased rocker design and pods placed strategically around the outsole allow for better push-off and smoother heel-to-toe transitions. The breathable engineered mesh material up top and plush padding in the tongue and lining help your feet stay cool and comfortable. This super cushy shoe that runs effortlessly is one of the reasons why RW shoe testers gush about it.

For those who like to customize their kicks, the shoe is part of the “Nike by You” line, allowing you to pick features like color and accents and even add your own text in the heel, tongue, and forefoot.

Sources indicate that you’re not just a runner. You also rule the weight room, enjoy a good cardio class, and have been known to dabble in metabolic conditioning workouts. If you’re looking for an all-purpose training shoe, Nike’s versatile Free Metcon 7 fits whatever your workout ask. This sleekly designed cross-training shoe lets you have it all, from supporting multi-direction movements on the gym floor to dynamic cushioning when you want to hit the treadmill.

Sources indicate that the shoe finds its multiuse purpose with a flexible design that features softer foam in the midsole and firmer foam in the heel for added stability. Plus, the full-length rubber outsole helps with traction on a variety of surfaces, including turf, concrete, and gym floors. You’ll also appreciate the webbed lacing and midfoot containment system designed to keep your foot firmly in place as you move around.

For those who want a mixed-terrain shoe that can hit the road and trail and also handle inclement weather like rain and snow, the Vomero 18 Gore-Tex is a great choice. These waterproof shoes are designed to take on puddles, pebbles, rocks, and roots without missing a beat.

The shoe has all the same stacked ZoomX and ReactX performance cushioning as the Vomero 18, plus a Gore-Tex waterproof liner to help your feet stay dry without getting too sweaty. The Storm-Tread outsole is specifically engineered for wet and slippery conditions, with an enhanced rubber compound for stronger grip and a thoughtful outsole pattern that keeps you grounded even on icy surfaces. Plus, the soft, protective mesh upper will keep your feet warm.

Sources indicate that if you are looking for a shoe to race in, the long-awaited Alphafly 4 is an revision to Nike’s popular carbon-plated shoe. It’s even lighter than its predecessor, the Alphafly 3, (approximately 6.6 ounces compared to 7.1 ounces respectively) and offers more energy return to help you chase your next PR.

That’s accomplished through its upgraded RF Air Zoom cushioning unit underfoot that uses vibration and frequency to create a smooth, comfortable ride, while the carbon fiber Flyplate gives you extra energy return to power through every mile. A slightly wider platform design compared to the Alphafly 3 also provides more stability so you can feel confident even on quick turns. And the wispy Atomknit 2.0 upper offers enough support to keep your foot firmly in place with as little added weight as possible.

It has been revealed that your shakeout run after a marathon or ultra should be about comfort at an easy pace. Think plenty of cushioning, a smooth, bouncy ride, and an unfussy upper. The Nike Vomero Premium ticks all those boxes, making it a good choice to slip on for post-marathon recovery runs.

According to recent reports, tired legs will appreciate a midsole that’s made up of ZoomX foam surrounding two energy-boosting Air Zoom units—one in the forefoot and one at the heel. The result is a light, comfortable ride with energy return that makes each step feel effortless and propels you easily along your route. You’ll want to wear this shoe for your daily runs for weeks after your 26.2-mile-and-beyond races.

Industry observers note that who doesn’t want to slip into something comfortable after a long run, or just a long day? The Nike ReactX Rejuven8 is just the thing, with a design that’s created to elicit all the aahs you can imagine. Thanks to React X technology in the upper and midsole, your feet will be surrounded in soft, responsive comfort. There’s extra room in the forefoot to allow your toes to rest and ventilation holes to allow your feet to breathe. Walking is easy and fluid because the sticky rubber outsole adds grip to the ground below you; therefore, no additional balancing act to get from one place to another. The result: A recovery shoe you’ll never want to take off.

According to recent reports, we all love getting gifts, but shopping for shoes can be tricky when you’re not the one who will be wearing them. A little advanced knowledge can make a massive difference in ensuring your present is truly appreciated. Here are some buying tips:.

Check what they already run in. If you can, look at the label inside a pair of running shoes they like, or ask someone who knows. Note the model, size, and width—running-shoe sizing may differ from their dress-shoe size—as well as any preferences, such as cushioning or toe-box room.

Check the return policy. See if the store has any specific limits on returns and exchanges, and if you can get a gift receipt so your giftee has the option to exchange the shoe for a different size.

Keep fit in mind. Remember that footwear largely depends on individual fit, with some shoes running bigger or smaller than the given size. When possible, avoid final sales (where the shoe is not eligible for returns) just in case there’s a fit issue.

The Nike running shoes best suited for long runs and marathon training are the Nike Vomero 18. You want to make sure your shoe offers both stability and support to reduce injury risk and protect your joints. Many distance runners today prefer shoes with maximalist midsoles, which feature a large stack of foam to cushion against impact, as well as energy return rocker designs for faster push-off and landings. These are all things the Nike Vomero 18 delivers on.

When it comes to race-day itself, especially for half-marathons and full-marathons, many runners seeking a time goal prefer performance shoes like Nike’s Alphafly 4, which have a thin carbon plate for strong energy return and maximum speed.

When looking for a recovery-run shoe, you want one that feels comfortable and provides plenty of support and a smooth, stable ride without being overly technical. The Nike Vomero Premium is the best Nike running shoe for easy recovery runs because it’s a shoe that delivers full-length cushioning and a roomy fit so your feet stay happy.

Industry observers note that to choose the right size and width for Nike running shoes, go to a store that specializes in running shoes and try a few pairs on. Most running stores will let you jog around the floor (and some even let you jog around the block) so you have a sense of what works best. Running shoes should feel roomy but not so much that your feet move around a lot. You should be able to fit about a thumbnail’s width between your longest toe and the front of the shoe. There also shouldn’t be any pressure on your pinky toe, and only a little bit of pressure on your massive toe.

Industry observers note that if you’re experiencing side pinching, bulging or spilling over, or flat arches, a wide shoe may be for you. These Nike models are available in wide widths: Downshifter 14, Pegasus 42, Revolution 8, Structure 26, Vomero Plus and Vomero 18.

#136972. Latest Update: 6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1487 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: 6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • To dial in your training, it’s important to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides.
  • Recent findings suggest that the formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr.
  • It has been revealed that over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To dial in your training, it’s important to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides. The catch? The most common formula for calculating max heart rate is not very accurate.

Recent findings suggest that the formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr. William Haskell and Dr. Samuel Fox in 1970, and it wasn’t necessarily validated by research and involved data from a wide mix of people, including those with heart disease and smokers. As a result, the formula tends to overestimate max heart rate for younger people and underestimate it for older adults.

It has been revealed that over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age). However, it’s still a rudimentary system—like, “might as well use an abacus as a bike computer” rudimentary, states Cherie Miner, M.D., a sports medicine specialist in Birmingham, Alabama. “It’s been the standard for years, but there are a lot of variables that can throw off your max heart rate.” Some of those variables: how fit you are, how hot it is, and how much stress you’re under.

According to recent reports, because of these variables, there are also a lot of myths surrounding max heart rate. Here, we debunk some of the most common ones so you can get to know your heart, and use your metrics to train efficiently.

Sources indicate that you’ve got to admit: This is equally horrifying and comical. But you can rest easy because it won’t actually happen.

“Most people have one to two minutes at their max heart rate—highly-trained athletes may have more,” Miner indicates. Expect to see your performance suffer very quickly if you try and maintain your max heart rate for more than just a short burst. Fortunately, years of evolving to survive prevents us from actually killing ourselves.

Industry observers note that the old-school formulas assume that it is the same, but Golich says it’s much more nuanced than that. Max heart rate is largely untrainable and determined by genetics—some of us have hearts tuned like humming birds’ while others have the slow-and-steady type.

According to recent reports, although not perfectly accurate, age-based formulas give athletes an easy and accessible way to find a rough baseline of their max without undergoing rigorous (or sometimes dangerous, in the case of a sedentary person) testing. That remarked, The American College of Sports Medicine suggests age-based formulas with a lower standard deviation, for example, the Gelish equation: 207 minus (0.7 x age) or Tanaka: 208 minus (0.7 x age).

According to recent reports, no matter which way you calculate it, your max heart rate is not an indication of performance, Golich says. “If your max is 200, and someone else’s is 190, it doesn’t mean one of you is the better athlete.” In fact, Golich has worked with numerous talented athletes at both ends of the spectrum.

It has been revealed that it’s good to remember that everyone’s max heart rate does drop as they age—but again, that doesn’t mean you’re losing fitness. Regular training and good nutrition will affect performance more than the fact that your max heart rate is now slightly lower than it was three years ago.

In a recent development, in reality, it’s not your max heart rate that determines your fitness level. Being able to hold your max heart rate for longer and longer sessions is what’s key.

Heart rate is a reaction to work being done, not a measurement of actual work. For example, Golich notes that if you ratchet yourself up to 200 watts (wattage measures your cycling power) for three minutes, for the first minute, your heart may tick along at 170 beats per minute (bpm). By minute two it may be at 180 bpm, and by minute three you could be pushing 189. But you’re doing the same amount of work the whole time: 200 watts.

If you were to ride for three minutes with the intention of maintaining the same heart rate, things would look different. Say you ramped up to 180 bpm to start—you might ride at 200 watts for the first minute, but you’d likely have to drop your watts to sustain that heart rate for minutes two and three.

Golich notes he prefers to have his clients train with power meters or using rate of perceived exertion (RPE)—a personal appraisal of how hard you feel you’re working—rather than heart rate.

“There are a lot of grey areas with heart rate,” he says, adding that being overheated, under-fueled, or even just hopped up on caffeine will throw your heart rate numbers off for the day.

Furthermore, the number displayed by your heart rate monitor or the screen on a gym treadmill may not be accurate. Sure, using a computer is certainly more accurate than the 220-minus-age formula, but Golich adds that because these devices take measurements every few seconds, they’re probably not dead-on.

If you really want to know your true max heart rate, an EKG is one way to go or a cardiopulmonary exercise test for even more accurate measurements, both of which require a visit to your doc or a lab.

Industry observers note that also, if you think that unless you’re hitting your max heart rate on every ride, you’re not working hard enough, here’s your license to chill. Max heart rate workouts should be done sparingly, Miner notes, since the ultra-high intensity can lead to injuries, extreme fatigue, and other symptoms of overtraining.

In a recent development, plus, there’s merit to working in many different heart rate zones—from increasing your base fitness with low-intensity sessions to pushing the boundaries at your lactate threshold, and even tipping into some anaerobic work. If you only have two speeds—hard and harder—you’re doing yourself a disservice.

Heart attacks, while rare, happen to athletes at all different workloads. Even so, cardiologist James Beckerman, M.D., states you’re slightly more at risk when working at very high intensities.

According to recent reports, “This is likely related to a combination of high heart rate, higher blood pressure with exercise (which is normal), and higher levels of catecholamines (hormones produced by the adrenal glands),” he claims. “For people without heart disease, exercising at higher intensity is generally safe.”.

If you’re someone with heart disease or who has exhibited risk factors, however, it’s a good idea to talk to your doctor about safe heart rate ranges for exercise and even get a stress test, he indicates.

According to recent reports, you’re not mistaken—your max heart rate for cycling really may be different than your max for another sport. Again, this is indicative of how variable heart rate is, Golich indicates.

Activities that are load bearing—like running—will generally push your heart rate higher, because you have to do more work to overcome gravity. Cycling, because it has the mechanical assistance of the bike, will generally produce a lower max heart rate. And swimming, which happens in a pool with zero-impact, may be lower still—since the water is keeping you cool, Golich says, heat will be less of a factor in raising your heart rate.

According to recent reports, what exactly is heart rate reserve? According to Miner, heart rate reserve is the difference between maximum heart rate and resting heart rate.

Your heart rate reserve can actually be a good measurement of how fit you are overall. “A higher heart rate reserve indicates better physical fitness,” she states. That’s because, unlike maximum heart rate, a lower resting heart rate is associated with better fitness. “If your resting heart rate is lower, then your heart rate reserve will be higher,” Miner says.

Tamanna K. Singh, M.D., is a board-certified adult clinical and sports cardiologist and RRCA-certified run coach. She earned her medical degree from Boston University School of Medicine and completed her Internal Medicine Residency at Boston Medical Center. She completed her Cardiovascular Medicine fellowship at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Newly introduced York, New York and her specialty training in Sports Cardiology at Massachusetts General Hospital. She is presently the codirector of the Sports Cardiology Center at Cleveland Clinic in Cleveland, Ohio and assistant professor of medicine at the Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine of Case Western Reserve University. To date, she has held several council roles with the American College of Cardiology (ACC). As a sports cardiologist, Dr. Singh provides cardiovascular care for professional, competitive, and recreational athletes and describes herself as an advocate for safe participation in sports. Media and print contributions include the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Time Magazine, and others. Outside of her profession, she enjoys running marathons, hitting the weights in the gym, playing sous-chef to her wonderful husband while cooking plant-based meals, and playing with her four beautiful dogs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, before you get on the treadmill hate train, hear me out. They can save your training, and I swear, they can be a ton of fun—really. Between the engaging, interactive streaming treadmill classes, and the ability to strip down to your skivvies and have no one see you sweat, it’s the perfect accompaniment to your marathon training, interval workouts, and even steady, zone 2 workouts. All from the comfort of your own home. And did you know that with many insurance intends, you can pay for your treadmill with FSA dollars? That’s a solid fiscal choice, right there.

There are a ton of treadmills on the market right now, and they’re better than they’ve ever been. They have more features, use less electricity, and are more versatile than ever before. Some are virtually personal trainers in and of themselves.

We’re in the process of testing a few fresh models, and we’ve just added the Urevo CyberMega, which is the first treadmill designed specifically for marathon training. It’s pretty freaking sick, I cannot lie.

Looking for a more heavy-duty treadmill that can handle higher speeds, longer miles, and more complex training aims? See our guide for the best advanced treadmills, which cost more but offer more training features and sturdier builds.

Sources indicate that there’s really something special about this machine. The NordicTrack Commercial 1750 treadmill hits that “Goldilocks-level” sweet spot with its cushioning—it’s responsive enough to save your joints without making your run feel like a slog or an unstable adventure. And with a 60-inch belt, even our tallest testers with their gazelle-like strides had plenty of room to stretch out and feel steady.

Sources indicate that our testers absolutely gushed over the treadmill’s sleek, streamlined design, especially the Z-shaped console with its high-perched 16-inch screen. It’s perfectly positioned for runners who like to stay close to the controls. While we wished the cup holders were a bit deeper for our oversized water bottles, the slim arms offered a surprisingly stable grip, even when our hands got a little… enthusiastic.

The 1750’s speed adjustments are pretty standard, going from 6 mph to a zippy 12 mph in 8 seconds. This is totally fine for 400- to 800-meter training, but for intense, quick-pickup speedwork, it’s not quite as snappy as some might like. Our testers did note one minor peeve: the lack of quick keys for 10 and 11 mph.

Industry observers note that we practically insist you dive into NordicTrack’s iFit program for an out-of-this-world experience. Our testers found its ability to read and adjust their runs to be nothing short of revolutionary during testing. While the high horsepower motor and Bluetooth speakers do make the machine a bit boisterous, it’s not at all distracting when you’re walking with your headphones on.

It has been revealed that despite its daunting price tag, the 1750 is a total workhorse that will supercharge your runs—and it goes on sale often. The built-in Netflix feature is a godsend, making miles absolutely fly by, and that cushioning is pure magic for your joints. Bottom line: the NordicTrack Commercial 1750 is a fantastic all-around package and a top-notch investment for most runners.

NordicTrack Commercial 1750 Review.

The Horizon T101 treadmill proves you don’t need a huge budget for a fantastic workout. At a sale price of just $600, this compact folding machine impressed us with consistent performance over weeks of testing. It’s a low-to-the-ground, 20- by 55-inch deck, ideal for casual runners 6 feet and under.

Sources indicate that the T101 boasts a three-zone running surface, offering extra cushioning where you land, less where you toe off, and a smooth transition in between for a supremely comfortable, low-impact ride. While it skips the fancy screens, its functionality shines. Connect to Strava or Peloton, or dive into workouts and courses via the free atZone app. Plus, there’s a perfect spot for your iPad to stream your favorite shows!

In a recent development, the six built-in programs are straightforward, displaying calories burned, heart rate, distance, speed, and incline (up to 10 percent). While it can hit a 6-minute mile, be mindful: the speed and incline dials are sensitive—one haptic notch, not a full spin, increases your pace.

But you know what’s a real showstopper? The T101’s incredibly easy, one-step hydraulic fold. Just lift the back, and it zips up. To release, toe the center bar, and it gently lowers itself.

In a recent development, for its price, the T101’s features are unbeatable. It’s not for marathoners or speed demons, but for everyone else, it’s a solid win.

In a recent development, horizon’s 7.0 folding treadmill is a robust upgrade, boasting a spacious 60-inch deck perfect for long strides, though its 20-inch width might feel snug if your mind wanders. Cushioning is excellent for long runs, but expect some bounce when the incline exceeds 5 percent—so perhaps skip the speedy hill work.

In a recent development, this machine is on the bulkier side, resembling a gym-quality unit, but its integrated features ensure easy setup. We loved the eye-level tablet holder, making streaming a breeze. Below, you’ll find a digital/manual console, fan, Bluetooth speakers, and two generously wide (if shallow) cup holders with room for your essentials.

Programming-wise, the 7.0 shines with its ability to link to Peloton, Apple Watch, and Samsung Galaxy watches, displaying calories and distance directly. Peloton classes synced smoothly, making transitions seamless.

A standout feature: knobs on the grips allow for effortless pace adjustments without breaking your stride. While there’s a subtle lag when decreasing speed, it’s barely noticeable at top speeds.

It has been revealed that at around $1,000 on sale, this treadmill offers impressive value. Its blend of convenience and comfort makes it a winner. Pro tip: opt for white-glove delivery—this beast is heavy, and assembly is a pain!

Full Horizon 7.0 AT Treadmill Review.

According to recent reports, marathon training demands months of relentless mileage, a crap ton of structured workouts, and more consistency than most of us think we’re capable of. The Urevo CyberMega is a treadmill that claims to be built specifically for the rigors of that beast of blocks. In a market crowded with all-purpose machines designed to serve everyone from casual walkers to occasional joggers to high-mileage baddies, the CyberMega is thinking of the needs of marathon runners first.

It has been revealed that that marathon-focused idea makes the entire experience. Rather than treating running as just one feature among many, the CyberMega is designed around the realities of high-volume training. According to the brand, every aspect of the machine is intended to support athletes preparing for long-distance races, making it a notably different proposition from traditional fitness-focused treadmills.

There are marathon courses built into the app that control your ‘mill, there’s AI coaching to get you to your PR, and a fun competitive leaderboard where you are up against other people. This treadmill is made to keep your training going when you can’t get outside and also? To keep it exciting. It is honestly fairly impressive and a ton of fun to run on.

According to recent reports, I was also impressed by how smooth the run is and how compact the machine is. It folds easily, stores without much hassle, and feels dang streamlined for a treadmill made to support hardcore training. That’s also the biggest drawback. If you’re over 6 feet tall, this is not the ‘mill for you with a 52-inch-long deck. But in spite of the short deck, it landed on this list is because it’s a wide-open area that doesn’t feel impeded by the bars.

The rotary knob is another nifty feature. It’s simple, responsive, and super convenient during workouts, and has speed and incline adjustments feeling smoother and more intuitive than traditional button-based controls or rocker dials. Overall, if you’re gonna be a world major chaser, you might want to think about chasing them on this ‘mill.

In a recent development, got a few runners in the family, or you’re a high-mileage runner? The NordicTrack 2450 is a seriously solid folding treadmill that’s got your back. It’s built tough, has great cushioning, and a huge 22-by-60-inch running surface, so you can just run without worrying about comfort and stability.

The Z-shaped handlebar and crossbar design are super minimalist, keeping the console right there when you need it, and giving you plenty of room to stretch out at the front of the belt.

Industry observers note that you’ve got your standard speed and incline adjustments, and this baby can zoom from 6 to 14 mph in under 10 seconds—perfect for those quick interval bursts. It has those quick keys like the 1750, but sometimes it can be a little tricky to nail down specific speeds.

Where the NordicTrack really shines is its iFit programming. We’re talking thousands of workouts, even marathon courses! Yeah, it’s an extra cost, but seriously, it’s a huge motivator. And that substantial display? It’s awesome. You can pause your run to squeeze in some strength training or even stream your favorite highlights.

In a recent development, fair warning, though: putting this thing together is a beast, so you might want to call in a pro. And while it’s not super loud, it might be a bit disruptive if you’re trying to sneak in an early morning workout while everyone else is still snoozing.

The ProForm Carbon TLX is a robust and dependable treadmill, designed for those who appreciate solid performance over excessive features. Its simplicity allows for focused workouts, minimizing distractions so you can stay in tune with your run. While it offers connectivity for phones, tablets, and fitness apps like iFit, at its core, the Carbon TLX is a workhorse—a no-fuss machine ready for you to hop on, get your miles in, and hop off.

Industry observers note that the treadmill features a responsive and cushioned surface that offers a pleasant bounce at higher speeds. Our testers found that despite the softer feel, the generous 60- by 20-inch deck allowed for a natural stride. However, I did occasionally feel myself drawing closer to the front console, so if you prefer more forward space, a different model might be better suited.

Recent findings suggest that for speed enthusiasts, the Carbon TLX is a dream. It rapidly reaches its top speed of 12 mph, and manual buttons provide smooth transitions between speeds. The incline goes up to 12 percent, providing a challenging workout that feels surprisingly good, even uphill. A standout feature is the powerful fan, strategically placed to provide excellent airflow—a detail any woman who’s done the “lift the boobs to get air” maneuver will appreciate.

If you’re a first-time treadmill buyer or looking to stay within budget, the Carbon TLX offers exceptional value for its price.

It has been revealed that the Bowflex T9 treadmill brings a punch of fun and functionality to home workouts, making it a standout pick for casual runners and fitness fans alike. The red center line on the belt isn’t just for show—it helps wandering runners stay in their lane, so every jog feels more confident (and a little less wobbly). The running surface is firm and comfortable, with just enough pep to keep things lively, while the compact, foldable design slides neatly out of the way after your workout adventure.

It has been revealed that the controls and incline? Well, they’re not winning any races. Adjustments take their time, so interval chasers might grumble about holding down those buttons like they’re cranking up a jack-in-the-box. But the T9 redeems itself with robust app compatibility—it syncs up with Peloton, Zwift, and even Apple Watch for gadget lovers, and has an oversized tablet holder for serious streaming or stats-watching mid-run.

Sources indicate that weighing in with a 350-pound weight capacity, a quiet motor, and speed toggles at your fingertips, this treadmill turns everyday training into smooth sailing. It may not be a speed demon, but the T9’s thoughtful features combine comfort and tech for an overall enjoyable ride.

Industry observers note that the Echelon Stride 6 is the treadmill I’ve kept at home after running over 1,200 miles on dozens of machines testing them for this article. It’s a solid, foldable treadmill that fits well in small spaces without feeling cramped. The larger-than-expected deck is 20.5 by 60 inches, giving plenty of room for a natural stride, even at my height of 6 feet. The deck provides firm cushioning that’s comfortable but not overly soft, which I definitely prefer for a closer to road-like feel.

In a recent development, the fold-flat design is a major bonus. The mill is stupid easy to tuck away under a bed or stand upright in a closet or—how I do it—up against a wall behind a curtain. That remarked, it’s heavy when folded upright, so moving it alone can be a pain. The treadmill has a powerful built-in fan and heart rate sensors, nice extras for longer sessions.

Overall, the Stride 6 isn’t flashy or cushioned like some high-end models, but it delivers a dependable run and great space-saving convenience. For a runner who values a firm deck, quiet motor, and compact footprint, it’s a practical choice that keeps me coming back.

Not everyone needs a treadmill for running, and we get that. Sometimes, what you need is access to movement and the ability to stay active all day long. Enter the Go Plus under-desk walking pad. It is the bridge between daily life and running.

I love using this walking pad when I am working. It’s calm and quiet, but allows me to keep my body and brain active when I'd otherwise be sedentary. It has a deck that is a wonderful size to fit under your standing desk, though I do think it could be just a teeny bit wider. It’s only about 50 pounds, and has wheels so you can maneuver it around your space easily. It’s remote-controlled for easy use, and best of all? You can store this gal vertically in your closet. (Just don’t forget about it in there!).

In a recent development, each and every treadmill on this list has been thoroughly evaluated by our team of editors at Runner’s World. I have personally tested each and every ‘mill on this list. Additionally, we solicited input from other staff at our office, like News Editor Theo Kahler, who has a PR of 14:20 in the 5K.

The team and I evaluated each treadmill, running for miles in every conceivable combination of uses. We evaluated how they feel, how well they change speeds and inclines, and even how they sound when they’re running. I then gauged that performance against their prices, customer service, and setup and delivery.On that note: I know that not everyone who runs is going to be able to move around a piece of equipment that weighs hundreds of pounds. As someone with a partially paralyzed left hand, I cannot handle the setup and assembly of a treadmill, so good customer service is a highly notable factor. I want to make sure that you’re not just getting a good ’mill, but a good overall experience.

It has been revealed that apart from general treadmill safety, there are a few questions you need to ask yourself before you buy the treadmill. These include how you want to use it, how long your stride is, if you want entertainment or training built in, and what you need as far as weight limits are concerned.

It has been revealed that having a comfortable treadmill means having one with a deck large enough to suit your stride. You don’t want to feel like you’re chasing to stay near the bar and not slip off the back, and you should ensure it’s wide enough that you can shake into your run without concern that you’ll step off the belt.

Having a running surface at least 20 inches wide is the bare minimum, and only for runners and walkers who have a consistent gait and few distractions when they run. It’s great for space to have a slimmer belt, but like running on a narrow trail, it requires concentration.

According to recent reports, the length of the deck is a trickier problem. What you need is largely dependent on the length of your stride, where you like to land in relation to your center of gravity, and your height/limb length. Having a deck that is too short puts you at risk for falling. Alternatively, it might have you trying to run up against the bar, which can affect your cadence and speed work, as you are essentially trying to outrun the machine instead of following its speed.

If you’re planning on using the treadmill for running, you’re going to want at least 55 inches of deck length. If you’re just using it for walking, 45 to 50 inches should suffice.

According to recent reports, if you’ve ever uttered the word “fartlek” out loud, you, my friend, need a treadmill that has easily adjustable speeds, and many of them at that. Do you need it to go all the way up to 12 miles per hour (generally the fastest speed on any treadmill) to hit that 5-minute mile? Probably not, but you at least want it to hit your top speed, and you want it to do it smoothly and easily.

Running is a sport of efficiency, and having to stop just to punch buttons that are not immediately responsive or are difficult to find will take away from your training.

Incline training is great for a lot of reasons, not least of which is preparing to run a hilly course. The majority of commercial treadmills offer some level of incline capability. Higher end models can reach a maximum of a 15 degree incline, designed to test the limits of your quads and glutes. Some models also give you the ability to do the opposite—offering decline modes—but those are pretty rare.

Recent findings suggest that treadmills offer more programming and entertainment than ever. Treadmills are no longer just a belt, motor, and bar. They are now Wi-Fi-compatible machines with programming capable of creating entire running looks and helping you execute them.

On-board systems like NordicTrack’s iFit are designed to help runners (and walkers) on their journey by providing them with tools like heart-rate monitor based workouts, whole-body fitness programs for runners, and responsive tech that monitors intensity, adjusting for your needs as you go.

Sources indicate that and perhaps more importantly for many of us, a lot of treadmills can connect to streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, Hulu, and more. Nothing will get you running quite so fast as watching Annabelle while you’re hitting your miles (though it may artificially elevate your heart rate, causing the machine to tell you to slow down).

Motors are a critical element to the design and function of the treadmill. There are typically two motors on each treadmill—one for running the belt and one to power the incline. The motor running the belt is the one taking the heaviest damage and using the greatest amount of energy, so it needs to be robust.

Speed and motors are closely related—in order to give the user an option to hit higher speeds, the treadmill needs a strong motor to keep up. Most motors are between 1.5 and 4 horsepower. We should note that the majority of treadmills with higher weight limits (north of 300 pounds) tend to have higher horsepower.

It has been revealed that we have found in our testing that higher-power motors can also take a lot more abuse, staying right and ready for more miles. Unfortunately, this does typically mean that the treadmill itself may be more expensive, but for larger-bodied individuals, distance runners, or speed runners, it’s worth the cost of admission.

What are the potential benefits for walking or running on a treadmill versus outdoors?

Industry observers note that it’s predictable. Greer says that it “allows the runner to precisely set and control all parameters, including speed, incline, and duration. This is especially beneficial for walkers or runners who are systematically progressing back into activity, either after injury, time away, new to running, or runners completing a specific workout.”.

Recent findings suggest that it also helps you stay consistent, which is critical when training. “Given the benefits of accessibility and predictability, a treadmill can help to promote a more consistent exercise routine.”.

What are some of the potential risks of treadmill training/use?

There are risks for specific treadmill injuries. “Recent literature highlights some differences in biomechanics between running on a treadmill vs overground. Differences in biomechanics result in tissues being loaded differently, specifically increased loading of the Achilles tendon with treadmill running.”.

Recent findings suggest that when you run outdoors, your body encounters different obstacles that help strengthen it. “Walking/running on the treadmill does not allow the diversification of movements and muscle activity required in comparison to outdoor walking/running. For example, up/down hills, turning, stepping onto curb or over puddle.”.

You might exert yourself more. There is evidence to suggest that “runners report a higher rate of perceived exertion (RPE) when running on a treadmill vs overground.”.

You need to know yourself and your limits to be safe. “Treadmills allow the walker/runner to easily increase the belt speed, however, make sure the speed does not exceed that which you are able to run safe and that you can continue to run with your normal running mechanics.”.

Tips for safe treadmill training?

Treadmills are a significant piece of exercise equipment, and they can be dangerous if not installed properly and monitored when in use. That is why we spoke with Ed Pryts, chief sales officer at Gym Source, a 30-year treadmill industry veteran, to learn the most important safety factors before you purchase a fresh treadmill for your home.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

In a recent development, jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).
