What’s the Minimum Amount of Core Work Runners Need Each Week?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A powerful stride depends on having a strong core.
  • But between fitting in runs, setting aside time for recovery, fueling, and living life outside of running shoes, it’s hard to know if you’re dedicating enough time to strengthening this key muscle group.
  • We asked experts for that magic minimum number, so you can boost your performance without carving a ton of time out of your busy schedule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A powerful stride depends on having a strong core. It’s basically the glue that holds your running form together and will make every mile more efficient, helping you hit faster speeds.

But between fitting in runs, setting aside time for recovery, fueling, and living life outside of running shoes, it’s hard to know if you’re dedicating enough time to strengthening this key muscle group. So when your calendar is already packed, what’s the minimum number of core workouts you need to do to reap the benefits?

We asked experts for that magic minimum number, so you can boost your performance without carving a ton of time out of your busy schedule.

Simply put, every runner should aim to get at least two 10- to 15-minute core sessions done per week, indicates Yusuf Jeffers, NYC-based strength and run coach, Hyrox race director, and Nike Well Collective trainer. This is an adequate number to support your running form, build more strength and power, and improve overall running efficiency.

However, several factors can adjust this number, including your running goals and the season you’re in, indicates Holly Dickinson, UESCA-certified run coach, NSCA-certified strength and conditioning coach, and owner of StrideHer run coaching. For example, if building strength is your offseason goal and you’re not running as much mileage as you would during race training, you might increase the minimum amount of core work you do to three or four sessions per week. During a racing season, though, you might stick to two sessions per week.

As for the exercises you need, you can skip moves like crunches, which can stress your back and neck muscles and isolate just a few ab muscles (namely, the rectus abdominis or those six-pack abs) and instead, go for moves like planks, bird dogs, Copenhagen side planks, and glute bridges. These moves help with spinal and pelvic stability and core muscular endurance, and mimic running form—plus, they work 360 degrees of your core.

Jeffers recommends spending at least 30 seconds on each move, completing your core work in a circuit-style fashion (which means completing each move back-to-back with minimal rest in between) and repeating the circuit for at least two sets.

If you strength train regularly, you probably don’t have to do any additional core workouts because many programs often require you to brace your midsection and keep your spine neutral in order to do the exercise properly, Jeffers adds, which is basically like built-in core work. Think of weighted back squats, deadlifts, and bench presses, for example. You need to engage your core to maintain a stable spine through all of these exercises.

Recent findings suggest that many people tend to think of the core as just ab muscles, but your core is literally everything that’s not your arms and legs, says Jeffers. That’s essentially everything from your abdominal muscles to your glutes, pelvic floor, and back. All of these muscles work together to keep you stable on your runs and prevent form breakdown.

“The stronger your core is, the better the transfer of power as you’re running,” Jeffers explains. “That can keep your form better over time and also improve running economy.” For example, marathoners who tend to slouch or lean too far forward in the final miles of a marathon may lack the strength and resilience in their core to keep their posture upright, which can then make running feel more difficult and lead to a slowdown, he explains.

You should consciously focus on your posture and form during moves like planks and glute bridges, Jeffers says. He urges runners to avoid compensating with other parts of your body in order to hold a given movement. For example, if you’re arching your back or sagging your hips in a plank, or you’re feeling the burn in your lower back instead of your glutes when you’re doing a glute bridge, these are signs you need to brace your core more and focus on a straight spine.

Additionally, avoid using momentum or trying to go through an active exercise with speed. “The second you feel like you have to use momentum or use other body parts to either hold a movement or to do the movement, that’s your cue that you’re not holding onto the form,” Jeffers adds. In that case, slow down your movement and focus on form rather than trying to reach a certain rhythm or number of reps.

“The convenient thing about core work is that it’s often done without any equipment,” Jeffers says, making it easy to fit into your schedule.

Recent findings suggest that for example, you can turn to bodyweight core exercises as part of a run warmup. Or you can add core moves to a strength session, like performing Copenhagen side planks between heavy squat sets. You could also save dedicated core work for the end of a heavy lifting session or for after an interval workout.

The key to reaping the benefits of a twice-weekly basic core workout is actually doing it regularly.

According to recent reports, oftentimes, you might look for a quick fix to a strong core, Dickinson claims, but keeping up with simple, frequent sessions is more effective long term. “Putting in the hard work is going to pay off, and it doesn't have to look extreme or crazy hard,” she says. “It’s about that slow, consistent work.”.

Experts agree that planks, glute bridges, and Copenhagen side planks are some of the best moves for runners. Incorporate these three moves into a quick routine two times a week to improve deep core strength and stabilization for faster, more efficient running.

Why it works: Planks train full‑body tension and teach your core to support the spine, just as you need on the run. By adding in variations like leg raises or shoulder taps, you can challenge your core strength even more and make planks extra functional, Dickinson told Runner’s World.

Why it works: Glute bridges allow for full hip extension, which leads to less strain on your back on the run and more glute activation, which can help improve—and add power to—your stride.

Why it works: This move works the obliques and hip adductors, or the muscles on the inside of the thighs that help draw the leg in toward the center of your body, allowing for better knee alignment on the run. Plus, they help with pelvic stabilization, which is crucial solid landings and forward propulsion.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your gym bag is probably packed with some of the best supplements for building muscle, including protein powder, creatine, and pre-workout. Crucial for boosting energy and strength during a gym session and reducing muscle soreness afterward, you wouldn’t dare train without them. But imagine a single supplement that combines the benefits of all three.

Recent findings suggest that enter XWERKS Motion — an innovative supplement formulated to enhance endurance during intense exercise and support a quick post-workout recovery. Sounds too good to be true? We’ll find out in this XWERKS Motion review.

It has been revealed that our team of personal trainers, CrossFit coaches, nutrition experts, and competitive weightlifters shared their feedback on the formulation, price, taste, and solubility of this one-of-a-kind product. As a registered dietitian nutritionist, I’ll do a deep dive into the ingredients and potential health benefits of XWERKS Motion, so you know if it’s worth adding to your supplement stack.

It has been revealed that medical disclaimer: This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. For health advice, contact a licensed healthcare provider.

In a recent development, our Breaking Muscle product testing team has tried nearly 20 of the best BCAA supplements, gaining a thorough understanding of what meets customer standards and what falls short. Here’s how our expert testers rated the following categories after trying XWERKS Motion themselves.

In this XWERKS Motion review, we’ll explore the product’s cost, formula, flavors, taste, and more. We’ll include honest, reliable feedback straight from our Breaking Muscle expert testers, so you’ll know exactly what to expect from this supplement. With transparency in mind, we include the good and not-so-good aspects of XWERKS Motion to give you the full picture.

It has been revealed that in comparison, Transparent Labs BCAA Glutamine costs $1.33 per serving, while Jacked Factory BCAA Powder is available at $0.67 per serving at the time of this writing. XWERKS Motion is on the pricier side, earning this category a 3.5 out of 5, but also contains ingredients not found in most other BCAA supplements.

XWERKS Motion is thoughtfully and originally formulated, earning it a 4 out of 5. It is unlike other BCAA supplements in that it contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbohydrates, also known as highly branched cyclic dextrin (HBCD). Cluster dextrin passes through the stomach into the intestines rapidly, where it can be absorbed into the bloodstream and taken up into muscle cells to replenish glycogen content and provide a quick energy source. (1).

Industry observers note that human studies suggest that when used before or during a workout, cluster dextrin carbs may decrease perceived exertion and enhance endurance when compared to maltodextrin and glucose, especially when prior carb intake is low. (1) However, those who eat plenty of carbs may not experience any added benefits when supplementing cluster dextrin.

In addition to carbs, each serving offers three grams of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). The product contains the BCAA ratio 2:1:1 of leucine, isoleucine, and valine. BCAAs are essential amino acids (EAAs), meaning you must consume them because the body doesn’t synthesize them on its own. Leucine is often thought of as the king of BCAAs because it activates muscle protein synthesis, which is necessary for muscle growth and recovery. (2).

Other active ingredients include calcium, magnesium, and sodium. During exercise, you lose electrolytes through sweat that need to be replenished. The electrolytes in XWERKS Motion help prevent dehydration and maintain proper muscle function during a workout.

Enhanced with natural flavors, sucralose, and citric acid, this product contains ingredients that add sour and sweet notes.

Sucralose is an artificial sweetener considered safe when consumed in moderation. Unlike table sugar, most research demonstrates sucralose has little to no effects on blood sugar levels or insulin. (3) However, some animal studies suggest it could disrupt healthy gut bacteria and increase inflammation when consumed long-term, but more human studies are needed. (4).

You won’t have any difficulty picking a flavor if you choose to try XWERKS Motion, considering there is only one option available — Raspberry Lemonade. Obviously, if you prefer to stick with one flavor on repeat this won’t be a problem. For those who like to switch things up, the lack of variety may leave you feeling bored, hence the middle-of-the-road rating on flavor.

Sources indicate that luckily, the Raspberry Lemonade flavor delivers. Our expert tester was more than pleased with the taste of the raspberry lemonade supplement, rating it an impressive 5 out of 5. She noticed hints of the tart lemonade with a more robust berry flavor overall. The supplement wasn’t too sweet and had a very refreshing taste to it. Our tester even went as far as to say that she could happily sip on this drink all day.

Another winning category of XWERKS Motion is solubility, which our tester rated a perfect 5 out of 5. She didn’t experience any clumping, grittiness, floaties, or difficulty mixing — a feature you’ll want when drinking it at the gym or on the go. Because the cluster dextrin in this product is highly soluble in water, it dissolves easily and forms a smooth, uniform mixture. Several customer reviews on the XWERKS website rave about the product’s superior solubility, mentioning it “blends so smooth” and is “easy to mix.”.

Industry observers note that cluster dextrin is believed to be safe for consumption, with no apparent safety concerns. (5) Our product tester didn’t experience any adverse side effects during her use of this product. As for beneficial effects, she didn’t notice any superhuman strength or noticeable bursts of energy, but she did feel good during longer lifting sessions.

Sources indicate that switching gears, BCAAs are considered safe when consumed in appropriate dosages. It’s best to adhere to the suggested dosage instructions on the product label for optimal safety and effectiveness.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, always consult with your healthcare provider before adding a new dietary supplement to your routine, particularly if you have pre-existing medical conditions or are right now taking prescribed medications. This precaution ensures that the supplement aligns with your individual health needs and won’t pose any risks or interactions.

All of the above considered, XWERKS Motion gets a 4 out of 5 rating for the lack of side effects from its formulation.

Unfortunately, there’s no mention of third-party testing on the XWERKS Motion product page, which is why we gave it a 1 out of 5.

We always encourage consumers to consider supplements that are third-party tested, because it serves as a quality control measure, ensuring that products are safe, effective, and meet certain regulatory requirements. Third-party testing enhances transparency and builds consumer trust by verifying that high-quality products contain what’s on the label and don’t include harmful levels of heavy metals or contaminants.

Sources indicate that XWERKS Motion and XTEND Original BCAA powder have both commonalities and differences. To start, both products contain BCAAs and electrolytes to enhance muscle recovery, reduce muscle soreness, and maintain hydration.

It has been revealed that however, that’s where their similarities end. While XTEND Original BCAA powder doesn’t contain any carbohydrates, XWERKS Motion contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbs for extra energy and prolonged endurance.

Sources indicate that XTEND Original BCAA powder also has a much higher BCAA content of seven grams, compared to the three grams in XWERKS Motion. The Original BCAA powder even contains a whopping three and a half grams of leucine, exceeding the recommended two to three grams per day to maximize muscle-gaining capabilities. (2) The same can’t be said for the leucine content of XWERKS Motion.

It has been revealed that customers on the XWERKS website give Motion a 4.4 out of 5-star rating. There are only 35 reviews on the product page. Motion is not available on Amazon at the time of writing.

One happy customer notes, “Great taste! No problems with digestion, gives you the fuel needed during most intense workouts.” Another customer says, “It mixes well, I like the flavor, and have no digestive or other issues. Performance-wise I feel great. I feel more energetic during my workouts and that I’m getting more out of them.”.

It has been revealed that reviews from customers who were less pleased with the product were written over a year ago, and the formulation and flavors may have changed. One customer says, “I’m not sold on this product. I don’t really notice any difference on the days I take this. Also, it takes a blender to get this stuff mixed! That’s a deal breaker for me.” Other customers complain of the grape flavor, which is no longer available.

XWERKS Motion provides a synergistic blend of cluster dextrin carbs, BCAAs, and electrolytes to support endurance and recovery during and after a workout. Those who enjoy leisurely activity and consume enough carbs to sustain their energy levels may not benefit from this product.

Sources indicate that however, it might be worth it for endurance athletes and bodybuilders with high training loads. Taking XWERKS before, during, or after intense physical activity may reduce perceived effort, extend the time to exhaustion, and decrease muscle soreness.

According to recent reports, you can consume BCAAs pre, post, or intra-workout depending on your fitness goals. Some prefer to take BCAAs before or during a workout to provide their muscles with amino acids to help prevent muscle protein breakdown. Others like to take BCAAs post-workout to support muscle repair and recovery.

In a recent development, if you eat a whole-food diet high in protein, then you likely consume enough amino acids and may not experience further benefits by supplementing them. If you struggle to eat enough protein, BCAAs may support endurance, helping you train at a higher intensity for longer. Additionally, BCAAs may reduce muscle damage and DOMS post-workout.

Industry observers note that BCAAs are a group of three EEAs—leucine, isoleucine, and valine— that must be consumed through the diet. They get their name from their unique molecular structure. While all EAAs are vital, BCAAs are thought to play an important role in protein synthesis, muscle recovery, and preventing loss of lean mass.

In a recent development, BCAAs may provide an extended feeling of energy and delay the onset of muscle fatigue, enabling you to work out longer. Moreover, BCAAs might diminish muscle damage, inflammation, and DOMS post-workout. Lastly, BCAAs may aid in preserving lean muscle mass during periods of fat loss, contributing to weight loss efforts.

Sources indicate that there are no official recommended daily requirements for BCAAs. The suggested sweet spot for leucine intake is often cited as two to three grams per day to optimize muscle building. (2) Avoid exceeding the recommended serving size on the product label. If you take protein powder or eat a high-protein diet, BCAA supplements likely won’t provide added benefits.

  • Think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish.

My friend Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, recently published an interesting article about the potential downsides of annuities. One of his observations is so simple that I think it's easy to overlook:.

Recent findings suggest that most Americans already have an annuity. It's called Social Security.

Think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish. You give up some control over a pool of money in exchange for a predictable stream of income, often for the rest of your life. Social Security already provides lifetime income, with the added benefit of inflation adjustments.

For a married couple receiving substantial Social Security benefits, that could represent tens of thousands of dollars of annual income that they don't have to generate by selling investments.

Tonal Review (2025): Our Experts Put the Smart Home Gym to the Test

📅 29 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tonal is a high-tech smart gym that makes starting an effective strength workout as easy as stepping into the next room.
  • It has been revealed that as a certified personal trainer and wellness product reviewer, I’ve tried (and stopped using) several pieces of home gym equipment.
  • Sources indicate that this Tonal review describes our experience using it, including details about the equipment, workouts, accessories, and other features.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tonal is a high-tech smart gym that makes starting an effective strength workout as easy as stepping into the next room. It has a cable resistance system with multiple attachments, so there is no need for additional equipment. You can choose between instructor-led sessions or work out independently using the demonstrations on the large touchscreen. There are a variety of workouts outside of strength training, including high-intensity interval training (HIIT), cardio, dance, yoga, Pilates, and more.

It has been revealed that as a certified personal trainer and wellness product reviewer, I’ve tried (and stopped using) several pieces of home gym equipment. I also work with a team of other expert product reviewers, some of whom have had Tonal for several years and still use it consistently.

Sources indicate that this Tonal review describes our experience using it, including details about the equipment, workouts, accessories, and other features. We also spoke to fitness expert Rachael Gonzalez, C.P.T., C.S.C.S., about Tonal’s workout modes and how they can benefit exercisers.

Related: Best Home Gym Equipment.

Based on our experience, we give Tonal an overall 5/5 rating. The only category where it didn’t receive a score is assembly, which doesn’t apply since professional installation is required.

Here’s a look at the scoring breakdown on a scale of 1–5:.

Sources indicate that we’re extremely satisfied with the Tonal equipment and programming. We can get a full workout without taking up a lot of space with free weights or having to pay to go to a gym and leave the house.

According to recent reports, the equipment is durable, and we haven’t had any issues. However, moving the arms can be noisy, which may concern people installing it on a shared wall. We had one arm that clicked slightly for a while, but following the troubleshooting instructions on the Tonal website helped fix it.

Recent findings suggest that some weightlifting moves don’t feel entirely safe or stable, so we usually replace them with ones we’re more comfortable with. The handles, bar, and rope accessories are comfortable to hold and easy to use.

Industry observers note that tonal automatically adjusts weight as you progress, which is really nice. Some workouts have a movement replacement option where you select a modification for the recommended exercise, which has been helpful in certain instances. For example, during pregnancy, you’re supposed to avoid twisting moves, so when one of our testers started lifting after her first trimester, she could easily substitute these moves.

Tonal has worked very well, and one of our testers says it has drastically improved her strength. When she started using Tonal in 2021, she was in the bottom 25 percent of all women. Now, she’s in the top 28 percent, and watching her score increase has motivated her to keep improving.

It has been revealed that the Tonal machine is a wall-mounted smart mirror with a built-in touchscreen and two adjustable arms that extend from the sides of the machine and can be moved up and down depending on what exercises you’re doing. You can choose between an on-demand or live instructor-led class or do your own exercises using the Free Lift option. Throughout each class and in Free Lift mode, a trainer explains how to adjust the arms and attach accessories and demonstrates proper form.

Workouts on the built-in workout app include weightlifting exercises such as squats, deadlifts, shoulder presses, lat pulldowns, tricep extensions, curls, and bench presses. The movement library has over 170 exercises to choose from. Each exercise is performed under the resistance of a cable pulley system using a bar, rope, or handle attachment, with up to 100 pounds of resistance per side for a combined 200 pounds.

Related: Best Functional Trainers.

Sources indicate that tonal recommends weights for each session based on an initial assessment, and your progress and performance determine adjustments. It offers unique weight modes, video form feedback, and floor workouts such as yoga and Pilates. The Tonal app also gives you access to workouts that don’t require the machine arms, so you can work out on the go.

Industry observers note that tonal uses artificial intelligence—Coach AI—to track progress, movement, and data from your workouts to make adjustments, weight recommendations, program suggestions, and more. You don’t have to worry about answering questions like: What do I need to work on today? What weights should I use? Should I focus on my lower body or do a full-body workout? Instead, one tap of the 24-inch touchscreen reveals an interactive library of on-demand and live classes or workout programs. Even in Free Lift mode, an option often used by experienced lifters, Coach AI tracks your data and makes adjustments and weight recommendations.

The first time you use Tonal, you’ll complete the Strength Assessment, which starts by choosing from the following goals:.

After selecting your goal, you’ll indicate whether you are a beginner, intermediate, or advanced exerciser and perform several movements—including a seated lat pulldown, seated overhead press, bench press, and neutral grip deadlifts—to help Coach AI get to know you and adapt to your needs, much like an online personal trainer. Your strength assessment results are used by Coach AI as a baseline when selecting the weight for each movement and to recommend workouts and programs.

Recent findings suggest that while this is a good starting point, it could be better. It’s hard to assess your overall fitness based on a single workout—what if you had an off day? Tonal addresses this by learning more about your strength level based on your performance in subsequent workouts and adjusting the weight settings to reflect your strength better.

During daily training sessions, it uses metrics such as time under tension, power output, range of motion, weight, and time to make weight adjustments and measure progress. Coach AI can detect when your form isn’t correct using your positioning, range of motion, and pacing. If it senses uncertain quality, it provides audible and on-screen reminders and feedback or turns off the weight. For example, the resistance shuts off if the bar tilts during a bench press because it suggests the movement is incorrect or unstable. If it senses you are moving the weight too easily, it increases the load each rep so you get the intended stimulus of the workout.

Another impressive feature is the four weight modes: Spotter, Burnout, Chains, and Eccentric. In Spotter mode, Tonal senses when you are struggling with a rep, lowers the weight so you can complete it, and returns the weight for the next rep to re-challenge your strength. Burnout senses fatigue and reduces weight until you finish the set. The Chains mode replicates the feeling of putting chains on the barbell by increasing the resistance during a lift’s concentric or shortening phase. Eccentric increases the resistance as you release the weight for more time under tension, which may help muscle growth.

Tonal enables each mode automatically during live and on-demand workouts. This automation creates a seamless transition between segments like supersets, where you concentrate on opposing muscle groups with little rest in between. If you want to work out with a partner, weight adjustments for both parties are automated.

Experienced experts lead each workout by demonstrating and talking you through set up and proper form. Even if you choose to follow the Free Lift setting or build a custom workout using the extensive movement library, there are video explanations of how to perform each movement. When you enable a specific weight mode, the weight is adjusted automatically, or you can adjust it manually on the screen using the dial. Interestingly, you can adjust the weight in one-pound increments, an uncommon feature in most cable machines and free weights, which typically adjust in 2.5 or five-pound increments.

To access these features, you’ll need a paid membership for $60 monthly, and Tonal requires a subscription for the first year. The only way to use Tonal without the membership is to manually set the weights to perform unguided exercises like a cable machine.

The purchase price of $3,995 includes the machine (which includes the touchscreen and arms) and no accessories. Aside from the floor workouts, most workouts use the arms and attachments, so Tonal isn’t usable without them. While you can use attachments from other brands, you’ll need to purchase T-lock adapters from Tonal for $43.

The smart accessories bundle from Tonal costs $495. If your budget allows, I recommend buying it because it includes everything you need to start using your Tonal immediately. Each accessory is available separately, so you can also choose what works best for you. Here’s a breakdown of what the bundle includes and pricing for each item individually:.

The smart accessories have a safety feature to turn the weight on and off with a button rather than by touching the screen, so you can position yourself before loading. The handles have a button on the side that’s easy to reach while gripping, and the rope and bar come with an attachable clip.

According to recent reports, as a beginner, our tester initially thought working out with Tonal was intimidating, but it’s a simple process once you learn how the smart home gym works. With a membership, you can choose between live and on-demand classes or a progressive program. Based on your Strength Score established in the initial assessment, the recommended weights are set automatically for you.

Sources indicate that from there, you follow the trainer’s instructions and on-screen prompts to set the arms and choose the right accessories for each move. Tonal automatically adjusts the weight, counts reps, and provides form feedback as you progress through the workout. There’s even an audible cue when you have two reps left, so you know what to expect if you’re facing away from the machine.

Industry observers note that free Lift allows you to choose from the library of movements and do as many sets and reps as you’d like. Much like the classes, the screen displays your live stats, and you receive a workout summary with your time under tension, range of motion, power output, and total volume lifted.

You can do floor workouts such as cardio, yoga, and barre directly on Tonal or by using the Tonal app on another device.

Recent findings suggest that strength training is the main draw of Tonal, so most of Tonal’s content focuses on weightlifting and HIIT training with weights. In addition to the four weight modes mentioned earlier, there are two custom modes:.

Recent findings suggest that gonzalez claims these options add variety and challenge, enhancing strength gains and training overall. “Diversification in your routine keeps you engaged and introduces fresh challenges,” she says. “Plus, variation can help you push past a training plateau.”.

Industry observers note that trainer-led workouts on Tonal automatically implement these modes depending on the intended stimuli, but you can activate them manually in the settings for any workout. You can adjust the weight at any point during your workout using the dial on the screen.

Recent findings suggest that “When training, I’m always super mindful of how my body feels and take it easy when I need to, so the Recovery Mode option would work well for when you’re sore or just want to move,” Gonzalez claims. “I really like the eccentric-focused mode. During the eccentric portion of a rep, the muscle lengthens while under tension,” she says. “The eccentric portion of a lift occurs when you are lowering the weight, moving against the opposing force of gravity, and research highlights controlled lengthening of the muscle fibers contributes to overall strength and muscle development.”.

In addition, there are several other types of workouts available on Tonal, including:.

Tonal has a massive catalog of guided workouts and workout programs and a library of over 200 bodyweight moves to allow you to build custom workouts.

In a recent development, the guided programs range from three to five weeks and focus on goals like improving overall fitness, gaining lean muscle mass, and burning fat. For example, Fundamentally Fit guides you through basic movement patterns, and House of Volume uses progressive overload to build strength. Many users on Reddit recommend Four Weeks to Fat Loss, a combination of resistance training and HIIT to maximize energy output. One claims, “Four Weeks to Fat Loss did amazing things to my body composition! Doing that program was when I really started to see a difference in how my clothes fit.”.

In a recent development, the smart handles help replicate moves performed with dumbbells and kettlebells, like hammer curls, bicep curls, or goblet squats. The smart rope can copy moves with a rope or chains, like pull-throughs or tricep extensions. Finally, the bar can replicate barbell moves such as deadlifts and bench presses. You can purchase accessories from another brand, but the smart accessories bundle from Tonal has Bluetooth connectivity, so you can press a single button on the accessory to turn the weight on or off.

According to recent reports, if you buy third-party accessories, you must purchase T-locks from Tonal to attach them securely. Additionally, you’ll need to turn the weight on and off directly on the touchscreen.

According to recent reports, tonal has a roster of expert instructors based in its New York studio and guest coaches who occasionally provide unique content. These fitness experts have diverse backgrounds, from competitive athletes to sports medicine.

Recent findings suggest that all Tonal-created workouts are instructor-led, so you’ll hear tips about form and safety throughout. Each instructor brings a unique style, personality, and expertise to the table, and Tonal users generally find instructors they prefer. For many, this provides the experience of working with a personal trainer, and several of Tonal’s past and current coaches offer personal training services outside of Tonal. For these reasons, Tonal allows you to filter workouts by instructor.

The Tonal app allows you to access your workout history, create workouts, and do floor workouts directly from your phone. The only thing you can’t do on the Tonal app is weightlifting workouts that require using the resistance cables.

According to recent reports, in addition, Tonal connects to several fitness apps, including Apple Health, Google Fit, and Strava. It also syncs with several heart rate monitors using Bluetooth, and you can connect to your Amazon Music or Apple Music account to stream or choose from the 14 stations on Tonal Radio.

Tonal has several features to help keep members engaged with the community and the equipment.

Recent findings suggest that first, there are several achievements you can earn for performing certain types of workouts, working out on holidays or birthdays, or reaching milestones like weekly streaks or 1,000,000 pounds lifted. Your workout summary lists the badges and milestones reached and your progress toward the following milestones. The Total Achievements Card shows how many workouts you’ve finished, the pounds you’ve lifted, and the longest weekly streak you’ve completed. You earn badges by trying a fresh workout type, training consistently, and working out at a different time of day. These achievements can be shared with friends and family using the mobile app.

The Tonal Leaderboard ranks all active exercisers based on how many days or hours they’ve used Tonal in the last 30 days, so the more you train, the higher you’ll rank.

Industry observers note that your Strength Score increases from the baseline as you get stronger and demonstrate progress during workouts. These improvements are calculated based on your historical workout data and are a huge source of motivation for many Tonal users. Using a percentage-based comparison, you can see how your Strength Score ranks against others, so some friendly competition is involved.

Tonal has a very active social media community if you prefer direct interaction with other members. The brand’s private Facebook community, The Official Tonal Community (OTC), has over 53,000 members and regularly hosts workout challenges and live discussions with Tonal trainers.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years, and she’s used it consistently the entire time, only stepping away briefly for injury recovery and pregnancy.

Before Tonal, despite being fully aware of the benefits of resistance training, she had no weightlifting experience beyond the occasional half-hearted kettlebell or dumbbell workout.

Tonal takes all the guesswork out of resistance training so you can lift the weights and reap the benefits, which is our favorite thing about it. You don’t have to worry about setting weights, planning workouts, increasing weights or reps, or tracking your progress.

At first, our tester didn’t understand Tonal’s difficulty levels. She thought the Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced class levels aligned with strength and fitness experience, but they correlate with the technicality of the moves involved. Beginner classes may include heavy weights if recommended by your Strength Score and the algorithm. The “beginner” aspect is that the workout moves are less technical, making effective strength training accessible to those who might typically be considered “casual” fitness enthusiasts.

Industry observers note that our tester says Tonal is a lot of fun. She’s discovered she loves lifting weights, and when she misses a few workouts, she gets antsy about getting started again. Tonal introduced her to barre, a ballet-inspired floor workout she’s grown to adore. There aren’t many upcoming floor workouts, which is sad because she loves the barre and pre/postnatal classes.

Industry observers note that our tester has attended live classes, but she doesn’t very often. Sometimes, she struggles with the pacing for floor/cardio workouts but finds the weightlifting workouts easy to follow. Mostly, she sticks to on-demand workouts because she appreciates the guided warm-up, exercise, and cool-down.

One concern users in the Tonal Facebook community raise is the lead trainer demonstrates the moves during a live workout, which is not true for on-demand classes. These workouts use the lead trainer’s voiceover and cut to another trainer demonstrating the exercises. This inconsistency doesn’t bother us, but some say it disrupts their flow or makes it harder to follow.

The instructors showcase their personalities, and none of the workouts our tester watched seem overly scripted or cheesy. Tonal recently moved their studio from California to Fresh York and replaced the coaching staff. Our reviewer had grown accustomed to the “old” coaches and still gravitates toward their workouts because she likes their calm demeanor. Some coaches have a bubbly, energetic coaching style, and others take a tough-love approach.

It has been revealed that these trainers have diverse professional backgrounds to support the workouts they design. For example, when our tester’s doctor cleared her to work out after a knee injury, she found Coach Liz’s workouts helpful because the coach is also a physical therapist.

Our tester completed several of the guided programs and saw consistent strength gains from each program. The programs can get repetitive, though, since many of them repeat the same two or three workouts for the duration of the program.

When our tester started using Tonal, her Strength Score was 133, and she was in one of the lowest percentiles of all female Tonal members. Although her progress has been slow, her Strength Score is now 354, and according to Tonal, she’s stronger than 82 percent of all female customers. Something about getting higher and higher in those percentiles is supremely motivating for her. In addition to her soaring strength, she’s experienced improvements in her mobility and range of motion.

Recent findings suggest that the base price of Tonal is $3,995, and the optional smart accessories bundle (which we highly recommend purchasing) is an additional $495. Professional installation, which is required, costs $295. Several owners on Reddit report signing a Release of Liability waiver and installing it themselves, but there is no option to remove the installation charge at checkout. Tonal often runs promotions and offers free shipping and installation.

Recent findings suggest that A subscription is required for the first year and costs $60 per month. You can discontinue the membership after one year, but you’ll lose access to many features.

If you purchase Tonal, the optional smart accessories bundle, and the required one-year subscription, the total cost of Tonal within the first year is roughly $5,500 before taxes, not including delivery and installation.

A monthly subscription costs $60 per month and isn’t technically required after you’ve completed your first year of membership.

You can only use Tonal as a cable machine for free lift workouts, and without a membership, you won’t have access to any Tonal content, weight modes, workout or strength data, history, or custom workouts.

In a recent development, the Tonal website notes professional installation is required. Before purchasing, you’ll need to complete a survey providing additional information for the installers, such as where to set up Tonal and the stud spacing in your walls.

If they determine you don’t have an appropriate place to install it, there are solutions. The brand offers wide-mount adapter bars and installation kits for metal studs. If you have concerns about where you can have Tonal installed, contact the brand’s customer service team for help. Typically, installation fees are $295, but Tonal occasionally offers free delivery and installation.

If you move, you’ll need to schedule a professional reinstallation. Tonal offers relocation packages for moving homes or simply relocating furniture to another room. Relocation fees range from $300 to $500 plus taxes, depending on your chosen service.

Tonal does not cover damage caused by attempting to install or reinstall the home gym, and if you choose this option, Tonal requests you sign a Release of Liability waiver.

Tonal offers a two-year limited warranty on the trainer and touchscreen, which covers parts, shipping, and labor. The smart accessories have a one-year warranty for parts plus shipping and labor. For such a premium (and expensive) piece of equipment, a five-year warranty on the device would be nice—and more comparable to warranties offered by other premium fitness equipment brands.

Tonal customers have had mixed experiences with customer service. Some say customer service swiftly and competently addressed their concerns, while others say they needed more urgency from the customer service team.

The Tonal website has several glowing reviews from its users, many of whom say they have canceled their gym memberships while drastically improving their strength and fitness levels. Several reviewers are excited about their progress and enjoy the objective tracking data from workouts.

Recent findings suggest that tonal has a 2.⅖ on Trustpilot. Several critical reviews mention installation, maintenance, and customer service challenges. Tonal partners with a third-party tech giant for delivery, installation, and repairs, and many concerns center around problems with this specific company rather than Tonal itself. Positive reviews mention the variety of workouts, convenience, and ease of use.

People on Reddit say they work out more frequently with Tonal and enjoy the extra time saved from skipping gym commutes. Several mention the cable resistance feels heavier than free weights, so the maximum poundage is not a limiting factor. One user claims they wish to see a floor-based alternative in the future for those who rent or need to move.

Sources indicate that tonal is ideal for people who are interested in weightlifting but need guidance and support to get started and see results. It’s a great fit for athletes and highly active people who want to advance in strength training to support their athletic endeavors and fitness goals.

In a recent development, likewise, many dedicated weightlifters have switched from using free weights to this comprehensive, versatile system. Tonal is an excellent option if you dislike going to the gym and prefer an all-in-one home gym solution.

It has been revealed that tonal isn’t ideal for people outfitting their home gym on a limited budget. For Tonal’s high price tag, you could buy a complete set of dumbbells or other free weights and other equipment or pay for several years of a gym membership.

Additionally, Tonal likely won’t be a good fit for advanced weight lifters already at or near the maximum of 100 pounds per arm offered for many lifts.

This machine requires adequate space to extend the arms to fully perform all necessary movements. If you live in a small or cramped space, it may not work for you.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years. Here are some of the criteria she used to evaluate Tonal when she first received it, and which are still very important to her two years later:.

It has been revealed that tonal and Peloton are very different but complement one another in several ways. Many Tonal consumers are also Peloton users since Tonal covers the strength training aspect, while the Peloton bike, treadmill, and rower provide heart-pumping cardio workouts. Each app offers live classes, and the monthly subscription to the Peloton App+ is $24, and Tonal costs $60.

The Peloton App One—$12.99 monthly—houses the brand’s floor workouts and has a much larger and more frequently updated library than the Tonal app. Peloton may work better if you enjoy these classes more than weightlifting. It’s more budget-friendly than Tonal, but Tonal offers a more comprehensive strength training system and programming.

Tempo is a smart strength training system and one of Tonal’s major competitors. It utilizes free weights outfitted with sensors rather than Tonal’s electromagnetic cable system.

Recent findings suggest that the Tempo Move—an equipment package with 16 weight plates ideal for beginner and intermediate use and a 12-month Tempo membership—starts at $963. It’s a more accessible system for people with limited budgets and has advanced features such as rep counting and monitoring form. Tester Jordan Smith, C.P.T., indicates, “It did a great job counting my reps, but it didn’t always pick up on my form.”.

The Tempo Move does not come with a screen, so you have to use your phone or other device, whereas Tonal has a dedicated workout space to stream workouts from an app. The Tempo Studio has a 42-inch display and ranges from $2,963–$4,463, depending on your accessory package.

Sources indicate that tonal can be incredible for your health, providing the structure and convenience needed to start and stick to a strength training routine. The fun programming, smart weight recommendations, and space-saving home gym setup make it a worthwhile investment for anyone interested in increasing their strength and who can fit it wisely into their budget.

Industry observers note that yes, after the first year. The $60/month subscription begins at installation and is mandatory for the first 12 months you own the machine. After one year, you can pause or cancel your subscription, and Tonal functions in “Basic Free Lift” mode, where you guide your own workouts. You can’t access your data analytics, workout content, or dynamic weight modes that provide personal training features.

Sources indicate that choosing between Tonal or free weights is a personal choice. Tonal has some pros: It’s space-saving and sets your weight based on your current strength level. Free weights are less expensive and don’t require an internet connection.

Currently, a Tonal membership costs $60 per month. Without the membership fee, Tonal works similarly to a manual cable machine.

Recent findings suggest that tonal weight feels up to 26 percent heavier than standard weights, according to one Tonal-affiliated study. The weight generated on Tonal maintains resistance throughout the entire rep, unlike free weights, which can feel lighter due to momentum and working with gravity at specific parts of the rep rather than against it.

No, Tonal is an independent firm and is not affiliated with Peloton.

No, Tonal requires a WiFi connection, even if you don’t have a paid Tonal membership.

Tonal smart equipment seamlessly integrates with the base Tonal model. If you wish to use your own exercise equipment, you can purchase special adapters from Tonal.

He Ran 3,067 Miles Across America to Set a Newly introduced Record, Averaging 73 Miles a Day

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Doing his best impersonation of the fictional movie protagonist who developed a passion for running, Balser, a 35-year-old red-bearded and straggly-haired ultrarunner from Indiana, spent the past six weeks spreading messages of love, joy, and kindness on an epic quest to run across the U.S.
  • Averaging about 73.6 miles per day, the Kokomo, Indiana, runner left San Francisco at 5 a.m.
  • His intent was to conclude his journey on the steps of Latest York City Hall, just as Pete Kostelnick did while setting his TransAmerica Run record of 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes back in 2016.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forrest Gump has nothing on Cameron Balser.

Doing his best impersonation of the fictional movie protagonist who developed a passion for running, Balser, a 35-year-old red-bearded and straggly-haired ultrarunner from Indiana, spent the past six weeks spreading messages of love, joy, and kindness on an epic quest to run across the U.S. in record time.

Averaging about 73.6 miles per day, the Kokomo, Indiana, runner left San Francisco at 5 a.m. PT on October 10 and ran across parts of 11 states before crossing the George Washington Bridge and entering Upcoming York City at 11:02 p.m. ET on Friday night. After running a few brisk miles through Manhattan, he eventually met up with his mom, stepdad, and two sisters and slowed to a walk on the final few blocks on the way to his finishing point.

His intent was to conclude his journey on the steps of Latest York City Hall, just as Pete Kostelnick did while setting his TransAmerica Run record of 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes back in 2016.

The only trouble was that when Balser arrived in Lower Manhattan with a gaggle of two dozen or so friends, family members, and random followers, they found all of the gates to City Hall Park closed and locked. So instead, he walked to a point adjacent to City Hall and, like Gump mythically did in Monument Valley, Utah, he just stopped.

Balser officially ended his relentless push across the country at 11:45 p.m., which means he covered the 3,067-mile journey in a record-breaking 41 days, 16 hours, and 45 minutes—roughly 13 hours and 45 minutes faster than Kostelnick.

“I know it was about the record, but mainly it was about us coming together and being together and loving one another,” Balser told the group around him after he finished. “We shared this experience, and I am so lucky and grateful to be able to do this, and I couldn’t have done it without so many people. I am grateful for this life and I’m going to keep living it like I do. So thank you so much, it means so much to me to have your support.”.

Shortly thereafter, his crew and family members celebrated with some late-night Latest York pizza and, after devouring a slice or two, Balser almost immediately crashed into a deep sleep.

“And we didn’t set an alarm for 5 a.m.,” crew chief Sam Yeary said.

Recent findings suggest that balser caught the running bug in high school and continued running competitively as a middle-distance runner for Vincennes University. He went through some hard times in his early 20s and dealt with depression that took him to a dark place that had him pondering suicide. But with support from friends, a job as wellness and housekeeping director at the YMCA of Grant County in Marion, Indiana, and an immersion into ultrarunning races from 50K to 100 miles, Balser got a upcoming lease on life and has been spreading joy ever since.

During parts of 2023 and 2024, Balser spent nearly 10 months running the entire perimeter of the U.S. self-supported, covering 11,170 miles at a much more forgiving pace of about 40 miles a day. He built a big social media following along the way, picked up a sponsorship from new footwear brand Mount to Coast, and started planning the TransAmerica run he claims he'd been thinking about for seven or eight years.

He planned to start in the spring, but his training suffered after he got sick, so he postponed it and began looking for a place to work and train. That’s when Yeary, a friend he met at a few Indiana ultrarunning races organized by Meshingomesia Track Club, offered Balser the opportunity to live, work, and train at his 60-acre family-run regenerative farm near Bloomington.

Recent findings suggest that training regularly with Yeary, Balser earned some money to help fund his journey, wrangled up a crew of friends and began making looks for October. He knew Kostelnick, a two-time Badwater 135 champion, had averaged more than 72 miles a day in 2016 to shatter the previous record Frank Giannino Jr. set in 1980. Balser decided to commit to running roughly 75 miles a day, which meant 15 to 16 hours on his feet with a rotating crew in a van meeting him about every four miles.

His route closely mirrored Kostelnick’s, taking him across parts of California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Nebraska, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Fresh Jersey, and New York. He passed over the Sierra Nevada range, across Nevada and Utah’s Uinta Basin, over the Continental Divide at Colorado’s Cameron Pass, and down the Poudre River Canyon, across the Great Plains and through Northern Appalachia, ultimately enduring more than 140,000 feet of elevation gain.

Things didn’t go flawlessly the entire way. He had some stomach challenges in late October and suffered from nasal irritation brought on by dry conditions. But for the most part, he was cruising along and following his catchphrase of “movin’ and groovin’” without any major setbacks.

“It was probably one of the toughest challenges any of us have ever done. It was absolutely insane,” Yeary told Runner’s World early Saturday morning. “We set a big goal this summer when he worked on my farm. We got to think big and dream big. He’s had this on his mind for a long time, but the stars aligned this fall, and we put together a blueprint to make it happen.”.

Balser was ahead of Kostelnick’s record pace from the start as his progress was tracked on the Breaking 42 website and Instagram.

Industry observers note that he was greeted by supporters at numerous points along the way and often joined by runners who ran alongside him for many miles. Yeary noted Balser and the crew were thrilled, humbled, and grateful to have so many Americans cheering on a couple of Indiana boys.

“Even as a crew, we were blown away by him performing at that level,” Yeary said. “It was hard, but it was necessary for us to treat his consistency for 70-plus miles every day like it was something normal. But we had to in order to keep things going. 70 miles is no joke!”.

In a recent development, balser’s effort developed an inspirational following on his way across the country. Social media engagement spiked over the final days of his quest, and more than 420 people watched his final miles through New York City via Instagram Live. Among those following along and offering support and congratulations on the live stream were U.S. Backyard Ultra champion Mark Dowdle and two-time Badwater Ultramarathon champion Lisa Smith-Batchen.

Sources indicate that “As an amateur recreational ultrarunner, I am so inspired,” mentioned Weston Traub, a San Francisco runner who was following along on Instagram as Balser finished. “Seeing him push the limits of endurance reminds me how strong the human spirit is. I have all of these long Strava routes mapped out in my phone that I’ll do ‘someday.’ Nothing crazy like running across the country. Seeing Cam get it done makes me think, ‘Do it now!’ Sometimes next year doesn’t happen, and life gets in the way.”.

Balser wore a YMCA of Grant County T-shirt while running through Latest Jersey and into New York City on Friday night. As part of his Breaking 42 campaign, Balser raised money through a website and intends to give 100 percent of donations directly to that YMCA branch.

“I know people really focus on the record, and, you know, that's a beautiful thing to go out there and set something,” Balser said. “But the main thing I wanted people to know is just that they're beautiful in the way they are. When we come together to do things, especially if it's something that speaks to our heart and what's possible with that, it's endless, you know?

“Keep your heart open and find the right people when your head's down to pick you up. I'm truly grateful. I have put my body through more than I probably would want to ever do, but, I know the reach of that, that love. Every step I take, every breath I get to take, it reaches more people, and that's a beautiful thing. And I think it'll ripple through my life and other lives. This record will be broken, but the feeling will last forever.”.

Brian Metzler is a Boulder, Colorado, writer and editor whose work has appeared in Runner’s World, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, Outside, Trail Runner, The Chicago Tribune, and Red Bulletin. He’s a former walk-on college middle-distance runner who has transitioned to trail running and pack burro racing in Colorado.

#136922. Research Indicates Cold Muscles Produce Less Power. Here’s How to Protect Your Performance on Frigid Runs.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1551 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Research Indicates Cold Muscles Produce Less Power. Here’s How to Protect Your Performance on Frigid Runs.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop.
  • Industry observers note that but what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction?
  • A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop. Both the research and anyone who’s put in miles on a hot summer afternoon can confidently tell you that much.

Industry observers note that but what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction? Does colder weather in the winter—ranging from just a bit chilly to downright frigid—take a toll on your running too?

A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does. According to the study’s authors, when our muscles get too cold, neuromuscular function becomes impaired. On the run, this can contribute to stiffness, less power output, and decreased endurance, all of which may cause your winter workouts to feel harder than usual.

The good news? You can still run strong when the temps drop—as long as you make a few key training adjustments before, during, and after you log your miles in the colder months of the year. Here’s how to do just that.

There’s no exact number on the thermometer at which runners can universally expect their power, speed, or endurance to decline, Stephen Cheung, PhD, the lead author of the aforementioned review, tells Runner’s World.

Temperature is just one of the many factors that contribute to how well we perform in the cold, Cheung explains. “It’s a function of the environment, as well as how much heat you’re generating, the speed that you’re moving at, and of course, the amount of clothing that you’re wearing,” he states.

Each of these factors varies significantly from runner to runner and affects how promptly their bodies lose heat. You only need to consider those in your run group who run shirtless when it’s freezing versus those who bundle up when it’s 50 degrees Fahrenheit to understand that we all thermoregulate (maintain our internal body temperature) differently. And the equation only becomes more complex when you account for wind and moisture—both in the environment and what you create yourself from air resistance and sweat.

Heather Milton, CSCS, lead exercise physiologist at Primary MD and cofounder of Master My Run, agrees. “It would be great to be able to say, when the temperature outside reaches [a certain point], your pace slows down by this many seconds per mile—but that’s not how it works,” she notes.

In a recent development, keeping this in mind, Milton indicates the cleanest reference point for runners to begin paying more attention to how they prepare for runs in the cold is when the temperature drops below freezing. Generally speaking, the colder it gets from there, the more noticeable the negative effects on performance will be, she explains.

Cold weather leads to vasoconstriction, Milton explains, which means our blood vessels constrict more, so the muscles farther away from the core don’t receive as much blood flow. If your fingers or toes have ever gone numb in the cold, for example, you’ve experienced the joy of vasoconstriction. Our bodies prioritize heating our core over our extremities because it helps our vital organs maintain a consistent temperature, which is essential for survival in dangerous conditions.

This physiological response, however, doesn’t bode especially well for running performance.

According to recent reports, “The cold slows nerve conduction so you have to work harder for the same power output,” Milton says. “And as temperatures drop further below freezing, that slower nerve conduction and the effects of vasoconstriction are going to be even more noticeable.” As a result, your overall exercise capacity decreases, meaning you may not be able to run for as long or at the same pace you normally would.

Industry observers note that what else might you notice when temperatures drop? “Physically, if your muscles and tendons are cold, they’re going to be tighter, less elastic, and you won’t be able to contract them as strongly,” states Cheung. “Stiff muscles can also put you at greater risk for tears or strain injuries.”.

Milton states this analogy, used by an old coach of hers, provides an easy way to understand what’s happening: When your muscles and tendons get too cold, they’re like a cold rubber band that can snap when pulled.

If you’re a runner who dislikes the cold, you might wonder if the smarter choice is to just run on the treadmill this winter. Don’t worry: As long as you prepare appropriately and use caution, you can absolutely continue logging regular miles outdoors.

According to recent reports, running well outside in the cold starts with warming up indoors first, says Milton. “An indoor warmup increases your internal metabolism and enhances blood flow, which helps prepare your muscles for contraction,” she explains. This also produces heat so your internal body temperature is more resilient to the cold outdoor environment.

According to recent reports, your winter warmup does not have to be any different or longer than your usual routine, Milton says. But you do want to make sure that you’re getting in a solid five minutes of prerun drills to adequately raise your body temperature and activate your muscles.

It has been revealed that she recommends starting with slower, more controlled movements that help activate the core and the glutes, such as planks with leg raises, lunges with rotation, and hip CARs (controlled articular rotations). Finish with quicker drills that require your nerves to fire more rapidly, such as leg swings and butt kicks.

Equally crucial to warming up is layering up—with an important caveat.

Industry observers note that when dressing for winter runs, keep in mind how you personally respond to cold temperatures, states Cheung, because everyone has different tolerances and susceptibilities. “I get very cold in my hands, so I’ll wear really thick gloves, even when I may be wearing relatively little on my torso,” he adds. “Pay attention to what’s an issue for you and adapt your clothing to both the conditions and your own peculiarities.” Cheung emphasizes this because you don’t want to end up sweating too heavily, which can then leave you chilled and clammy.

Industry observers note that if you need a starting point for your winter running wardrobe, aim for two to three layers of breathable, moisture-wicking fabrics. If possible, choose a wind- and water-resistant shell for your outermost layer, suggests Milton. For your lower body, wear shorts over your tights to help keep your glutes warm. Finally, cover any exposed skin on your head, ears, and hands, and opt for a pair of wool socks—all of which can help ensure adequate blood distribution to the extremities, Milton adds.

When you head out for runs in the cold, slowly build up to your usual pace.

Recent findings suggest that gradually easing into your workout gives your muscles more time to adjust, and it can also help your airways get used to the colder temperatures, Milton indicates. You don’t necessarily need to go slower for your entire run, but you should try to match your rate of perceived exertion (RPE) with your typical effort, rather than aiming for your usual pace or heart-rate zone.

“Think about it the same way as if you were running on an extremely hot day,” Milton says. “Let’s say your RPE for an easy run is about 3 out of 10. Keep that 3 out of 10, even if your pace is a little slower.”.

In a recent development, if you find that your run feels more difficult than usual, slow down if you need to, but don’t stop completely, Cheung advises. “Don’t take long breaks, because that’s when you aren’t generating as much heat. Just keep moving so you have that constant heat generation,” he says.

If you start to get cold on a run, try speeding up a little bit to stoke that metabolic heat production, Cheung says. But make sure you do it safely: Don’t force the effort in icy conditions or when your muscles feel especially stiff. Scouting out run routes with more tree coverage to block wind on blustery days can also help you stay warmer, he adds.

As soon as you finish your workout, change out of your sweaty running gear and into warm, dry clothes, Milton claims.

Even if you’ve only sweated a small amount—for example, maybe you just have some dampness under your armpits—you still want to remove any wet fabrics against your skin. “Even that small amount of wetness can start to drop your core temperature,” Milton explains. If you wait until you’re near shivering, you’ll face an uphill battle to get yourself warm again.

You can also opt for a relaxing shower and hot chocolate—extra marshmallows.

Sources indicate that morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

Recent findings suggest that A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.
